utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I return this to the registry. Thank you. Mr. Sayers, and indeed Dr. Almond, I'm sorry to have kept you waiting, but we had to consider the circumstances of another case which we may have to deal with. But we're now ready. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One very brief preliminary matter, Mr. President. The batting order for witnesses this week is as stated in my letter of June 21st, the most recent letter, with the exception of witness number 4 on that list, who is not available. And with the Court's permission, Mr. Browning will take the direct examination of the first two witnesses on the list, Mr. Almond and Dr. Mestrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Browning:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, could I have you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: My name is Mark Padrais Almond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Almond, do you have a copy of your report that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make a pause between question and answer for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I do have a copy of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: May I ask you first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, you're being asked to make a pause between the question and answer, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I will do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It needs to be remembered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, if I could ask you to turn to your curriculum vitae. And the Court has your credentials before it, but there are a couple of brief points that I would like you to clarify. First of all with regard to the fourth line on the first page of your curriculum vitae, if you could explain to the Trial Chamber the time period that you've been a lecturer in modern history at Oxford University.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I've missed out a dash which would indicate that from 1986 until the present day I'm a lecturer in modern history at Oriel College in Oxford. I apologise for that, if that misleads anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you received your degree from Oxford University in 1980 and have worked continuously, either as a researcher or a lecturer, in the field of history?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have numerous publications listed in your curriculum vitae dealing with the former Yugoslavia and eastern Europe. Do you have any publications currently in progress?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: For the Hoover Institution, I have a project which is essentially dealing with matters to do with the American media, and one part of it will be dealing with the relationship between interpretation of international relations and political decision making. That's the part that will be relevant to the former Yugoslavia, in part, in part, although only in part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I notice on the second page of your curriculum vitae you've been a frequent commentator on various television programmes, as well as radio, as well as a frequent commentator on affairs of the former Yugoslavia and various newspapers and other publications. Could you give us an idea of the frequency by which you've been referred to in newspapers and appeared on television with regard to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Depending upon the state of events in the former Yugoslavia, or other areas where my views are requested, the degree of frequency varies, but quite often if there is a particular event or series of events taking place, it may be not only once a week, but several times even in a day, for the BBC's various news channels but also for other channels like CNN, SKY News, and Channel 4 News. Also I get asked to write in newspapers. So there may be periods generally -- certainly, even in a relatively quiet period, I would be asked once or so a month, and quite frequently, as I say, several times a week or even a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report that you have before you that has been filed with the Trial Chamber, is that a full and accurate summary of your opinions and conclusions in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. The report expresses my opinions and conclusions. There may be certain, I regret to say, certain typographical errors as a result of the time factor, which prevented me from revising the report which I had to submit from Washington D.C., but the text represents my interpretation of the matter as fully and accurately as I could present it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as set out in the first sentence of that report, you agree with many of the historical facts contained in the report of Robert Donia but disagree with some of the conclusions and opinions that he has reached?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. Much of what Dr. Donia says is true, and certainly much of the history is unimpeachable. On the particular conclusions about the events really of 1991, 1992, the breakup of Yugoslavia and how that is to be interpreted, in this particular area I diverge from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you also diverge from him with regard to the historical significance of the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you explain the historical significance of those borders and how your opinions and conclusions differ from Robert Donia?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think that under the impact of the terrible events in Bosnia-Herzegovina after 1992, when the Serbs caused such suffering to primarily the Muslims, a lot of people, including the smaller community, adopted a myth, a benign myth, but nonetheless a myth, of the historical continuity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which I myself concede is a very tempting idea. And the apparent continuity of particularly the northern and western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina over recent centuries is introduced in evidence I think in this Court but also in public discussion, in books and newspaper articles, that there was a natural political civic entity of Bosnia-Herzegovina which ran back through time. It seems to me that this overlooks that the real reason why those borders existed between the Habsburg or Austro-Hungarian Empire and the Ottoman Empire was precisely great power politics, but there may have been peculiar geographical features that led to different states and political entities at different times choosing those boundaries largely as the ones to be the basis of their division. But that the interests and the wishes of the populations on either side of those boundaries were not in the minds of the diplomats and politicians, whether in Istanbul or in Vienna/Budapest, who devised those boundaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what significance do those boundaries have when events transpire in 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The boundaries of the internal republics of the collapse in Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia of course cut across the ethnic lines. I use "ethnic" here not necessarily to mean that there was -- in the scientific sense, but I think it's common parlance to describe Croats, Serbs, and Bosnian Muslims as different ethic groups. So the cultural, economic and a variety of other traditional links which cut across these boundaries were not necessarily regarded as natural by significant groups of people; Croat and Serb on either side. Also, I might add, Bosnian Muslims regarded the Sandzak of Novi Pazar which lay outside of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina either as part of Yugoslavia before 1991, 1992 or as an independent state since. They regarded that territory as being inhabited largely as people who they saw as being of common identity with themselves. So in short, although there may be very good and desirable reasons for the creation of a Bosnian-Herzegovinian on the basis of the republican boundaries in 1991, it is not inherently pernicious to question those boundaries and indeed representatives of all three groups at different times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain the historical significance of the meeting in Karadjordjevo between President Tudjman and President Milosevic and particularly the events that one must consider subsequent to that meeting in interpreting Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think that the attention of this meeting is out of proportion to its significance. If one judges not what is rumoured and alleged to have been agreed of subsequent events, then the allegations of some kind of conspiracy plan to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of the wishes of its inhabitants between Croatia and Serbia that such a plan was hatched and prepared and this meeting is not borne out by subsequent developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the subsequent developments --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The subsequent developments are that Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pardon, Mr. Browning. What you have just mentioned about the meeting, you said that has not been confirmed or been borne out [no interpretation]. Could you speak to the meeting itself without mentioning as the events that were to take place later on, because you seem to say that the further developments failed to confirm that there was a plan to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina, but as to the meeting itself, was that kind of plan mentioned at all, whatever the further developments may have been? So this is the first question of primary interest before we speak about the further developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, if you could, please, explain what you as a historian and historians in general know with regard to the meeting in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: With regard to that meeting, there are -- various sources have appeared primarily on the part of Croats. To the best of my knowledge, neither Mr. Milosevic nor any of the Serbian participants have given an account of this meeting. The problem with the sources which are all in the public domain that I know of from the Croatian side is that they are all from sometime after the events, after the particular meeting. Even if we go back to the spring of 1991, in addition to the meeting between President Tudjman and Milosevic, there were also discussions about how the future of Yugoslavia was to be developed on the part of the heads of government and other political actors in all the member states so that, for instance, President Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia held discussions with Milosevic, Slovenes too. It was not self-evident at that time that the republican boundaries of the then waning Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia would be treated as sacrosanct by the International Community as one actor so that discussions about the complex ethnic map and how that might or might not affect the future development of the individual republics either as part of a reconstituted or reformed Yugoslavia or as independent states. All of this was clear in March 1991 and was very much up for grabs. I think it is very important to remember, and this is a problem that historians always have that the events that took place that we know about, though specific details may be disputed, were not known at the time, though nobody knew at the time what was to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but the question that I asked you and you didn't answer my question, the simple -- it was simple. As an expert, as a historian who must have studied this period on the basis of available documents, what do you think as an expert at that meeting between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic? What happened during the course of that meeting? Do you have any idea? You say you do not have any idea, that is all right but you, yourself, have you formed an opinion as to what happened and what was said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: My opinion is that there was an inconclusive discussion which included the question of if Yugoslavia was to breakup, would Bosnia be -- what would be the future status of Bosnia and one aspect of that discussion, I suspect, on the basis is would it be divided between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia. On the substantive point of whether any conclusion was reached about how to do that, I think that no evidence that such an agreement let alone plan or timetable was developed and that if subsequent events suggest to me that insofar as President Milosevic of Serbia was entering into such a discussion with Croatia, it was partly in the context of his own internal difficulties in March of 1991. There had been large-scale demonstrations against the rule of the -- Serbian Socialist Party and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Almond, is it possible for you or Robert Donia or any other historian to say with precise absolute precision what was agreed to at Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It's not only possible to say with any precision, I think, it is, in fact, impossible to say that there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, of course ultimately this is a matter which we are going to have to determine or may be for the purposes of our judgement as a matter of fact, as a finding of fact whether there was an agreement or not. But I'm not going to stop you asking the witness about his opinion about it but we'll have to decide it on the evidence such as it is, that is, put before us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a historian and interpreting the events in Karadjordjevo, you had referred to subsequent events and how that must be considered as a historian in evaluating whether there was a plan to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you set out the subsequent events that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The idea of collusion between Croatia and Serbia seems to me to fall down on the fact that the Croatian republic was a victim of an attack by the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, and also local Serb forces in the Krajina, Slavonia, and so on, I believe organised to a great extent and directed by the Belgrade government. And therefore, the idea that there was a persistent cooperation between Zagreb and Belgrade must fall down on the actual military developments which included large-scale destruction of property and ethnic cleansing of Croats. I might make the point if I may, also, that already in August of 1990, the certain Serb forces, paramilitary forces in Krajina and parts of Slavonia had been organised in -- to form an interaction against the newly-elected government of Croatia, and I think that many of the historians who might not necessarily agree with me on every point would agree that that, too, was largely steered from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent must one consider the destruction of Vukovar in August 1991 and the attack on [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The destruction of Vukovar in the later part of 1991 and also the bombardment of Dalmatian cities and territory seems to me also to compound the problem of the idea of collusion. Most observers in the summer and autumn of 1991, I believe, concluded that the strategy both of Belgrade, of the still existing federal authorities and of Mr. Milosevic's government, the government of Serbia, which was increasingly the dominant force, was to effectively destroy the viability of the Croatian republic as a nascent independent state by occupying large place or territory, by creating economic turbulence because of refugees, and the destruction of infrastructure and destroying its tourist trade which has never fully recovered from the onslaught on coastal towns, and it was a very important part of the economy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In evaluating significant events, what significance should be given to Croatia's recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Croatia's recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina is quite important because, first of all, Croatia was the first state to do so at a time when, for instance, the United States was still -- whose policy was still very unclear. Furthermore it is worth remembering that when Slovenia, then Croatia, declared their independence from Yugoslavia at the end of June 1991, Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was under a government elected in 1990 led by Alija Izetbegovic, did not, certainly not in the eyes of Croats, act in a way that was sympathetic or helpful to the Croats in their conflict with the JNA and with the local Serb paramilitaries. So that this gesture of recognition was not wholly reciprocal; it was in fact an unilateral act, if you like, by Zagreb to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina though many Croats felt that the Bosnians had not assisted them when they were under attack by similar forces to those now attacking Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a historical fact, Croatia also sent ambassadors to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you mentioned that Croats saved Muslims at crucial times. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: If we look at the -- I'm sure you're familiar with the maps -- strategically the territory controlled by the Bosnian government was dependent upon supplies and assistance from the Croatian territory -- from the territory of the Croatian republic. Without that flow of humanitarian aid and other supplies through Croatia, the Bosnia-Herzegovina government would have been incapable of even the limited resistance that it was able to put up to the attack by the Serbs. More precisely, in the summer of 1995, when the Bosnian Serb army launched its offensive against the so-called UN protected safe areas, Zepce, Srebrenica, moving on to Gorazde, and also Bihac, if the Croatian army and also local Croatian forces within Bosnia-Herzegovina had not intervened at a time when the international community, NATO, did not act and only acted subsequent to the actions of the army of the Croatian republic, I believe that Bosnia-Herzegovina's so-called Muslim government and its territories would have been almost entirely overrun. In the course of an interview with President Izetbegovic in November of 1996, he was asked if he put President Tudjman and President Milosevic on the same level as aggressors against Bosnia-Herzegovina and he explicitly said that though there had been very hard times between the Bosnian government and the Croats over the issues of obviously the basis of this trial, the key point that he mentioned was that unlike Milosevic, Tudjman had been in a position to strangle Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim government, and had not done so. I think this also reflects upon the idea that there was a persistent conspiracy from 1991 onwards to do that that the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not feel that whatever difficulties he had had with the Croats, that that was what was being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The discussion that you just referred to was actually a discussion that you personally attended?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes, with certainly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Along with a number of scholars and people who had been interested in the war from 1991 to 1995 and who had written about the conflict, I was invited to a conference in Sarajevo and at the conclusion of the conference we were invited to meet President Izetbegovic and held approximately an hour-long discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Karadjordjevo, I believe in your report you referred to it as a dog that did not bark. Could you explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Dr. Donia expresses the opinion that Karadjordjevo is symbolic of collusion between Croatia and Serbia to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina. My understanding of developments after that is that whatever was discussed, it was not a plan for the forcible partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that did not occur. And on the contrary; it was initially Croatia that was threatened with either large-scale territorial losses, or even destruction, within weeks of this meeting. And I would put the meeting at Karadjordjevo in the context of other meetings between leaders and other political figures in Yugoslavia of the different republics trying to come to some kind of agreement about the future of Yugoslavia and sadly failing. And out of that failure came the conflict, which I believe was largely the result of the aggression or the deliberate use of force by the Serbs and the JNA, first of all in Slovenia, then in Croatia, later in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to the conflict, I believe that you refer in your report to the strain that developed between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims as a result of the position that was taken by Bosnian Muslim leaders as the war began in Croatia. Can you explain that concept, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: When the fighting broke out in Slovenia, the Slovenes said, "Why didn't the Croats come to our aid?" When the fighting broke out in Croatia, despite the precedent already in Slovenia, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina not only did not seek to frustrate the military operations of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serb forces using its territory as a logistics and other form of base for the attack upon Croatia, but in certain regards it de facto cooperated with what after all was still the army of the state of which it was a constituent republic. So that, for instance, no doubt with the intention of trying to forestall an attack upon itself, or certainly to give no excuse for such an attack, the arsenals, the weapons of the Territorial Defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were instructed by the government to be handed over to the JNA. A concurrent problem that helped to foster distrust between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats and Croats in general in the Bosnian government was that several officers of the JNA who participated in the conflict against Croatia very soon afterwards became officers in the nascent army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or military advisors to President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also explain the significance of the uncertainty regarding independence and what you described as the ambiguous public stand of President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Not least because he and his colleagues had witnessed the terrible violence, the onslaught on Croatia, the ethnic cleansing in Vukovar and so on, president Izetbegovic was anxious to avoid such conflict, and he recognised that many of the ingredients for such a conflict existed. However, his efforts, which I believe were sincerely well-intentioned to avoid such a conflict, nonetheless naturally aroused fears amongst the Croatian community in Bosnia-Herzegovina that their interests, and also their sense of solidarity with fellow Croats in Croatia itself, might be sacrificed in the course of discussions, which, after all, were secret, behind closed doors, or on telephone lines, between Sarajevo and Belgrade. So that there was a climate of anxiety fostered by this, not least because, as I say, at the time when Croatia itself and many Croat civilians were the subject of a very bitter onslaught by the JNA and Serb forces, the Bosnian government was at best passive, and at worst cooperated, from the point of view of Croats, with their enemies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report you refer to Muslim forces regarding Bosnian Croat areas as areas where they could gain compensation for territory lost to Serbian forces. Could you explain that concept.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Part of the underlying tragedy of this conflict between Croats and Bosnian Muslims is precisely the strategic goal of the Bosnian Serbs. They had launched an onslaught which had caused intense suffering and huge displacement of people, particularly from eastern Bosnia but from other parts that they controlled, and those people were funnelled into areas which had been largely untouched by the conflict. It is not the first time in history, tragically, that people who are victims do not necessarily feel obliged to behave entirely according to what we might think of as the principles of natural justice towards a third party. On the contrary; I'm afraid it seems to me that not only having been driven from their homes -- including, of course, the soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were themselves refugees very frequently, as well as their families, many of whom they were not certain of their fate -- that having been driven from their homes and having no reason to believe they would return home, particularly given the repeated statements by the International Community that it was not going to reverse ethnic cleansing by force, in that situation there arose the -- in a certain sense it is natural, but highly undesirable response of saying, "Well, here is relatively undefended territory in which we are now coming as refugees which we should occupy for ourselves." And I think again historians probably would agree that it's a common phenomenon in conflict that those people who have been either directly in conflict with soldiers or affected by it as civilians very frequently have great resentment towards non-combatants, behind the lines, who are not directly affected by the war. And in this case the civilian population of Central Bosnia, for instance, had been mercifully immune to conflict compared with what had happened either in parts of Croatia itself or in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina largely inhabited -- or where the victims were largely Bosnian Muslims. And this phenomenon, as I say, I think is unfortunately an undesirable but natural phenomenon. It was part, however, of the Serbian strategy to not only drive the Muslims and, in those places where they lived, Croats, out of territory which the Bosnian Serbs wished to control, but also to foster conflict between those two groups. I note, for instance, that Dr. Donia quotes from Tanjug at one point on -- Tanjug, the Yugoslav Belgrade-based news agency, as a source for the antagonism between Croats and Muslims. That seems to me, arguably, to be a deliberate source of propaganda designed to exacerbate and promote conflict between Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: See if I can follow this. The point you're saying is that it was part of Serb strategy to foster a conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. Because, first of all, if we remember the context, although the principal government involved with the UNPROFOR operation, Britain and France, their public spokesman said they did not wish to become involved in the conflict, there was a great deal of public pressure, including from parliamentarians, from people writing in the press -- I include myself in that -- saying that the conflict was primarily one in which Serb forces, steered largely from Belgrade, were engaged in aggressive and criminal acts against the civilian population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I quote some of this in my report. Public demands by the leader of the labour opposition, in Britain, for instance, are the politicians, including occasionally conservative politicians, for military intervention. In that context, the Serbian government and Serbian forces had an interest in creating or promoting a conflict between Croats and Muslims so that the argument which had been raised from the very beginning by people who tended to be sympathetic to Belgrade that really all the people in the Balkans, in the former Yugoslavia, were given to atrocities, were given to aggressive ambitions, that this would come about. And partly as a result simply of their own conquest. The Serbs created the context in which there would be conflict for resources, for accommodation, between the largely Muslim refugees coming into territories which they had not lived in before which were, in particular places, largely Croatian inhabited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Browning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along those lines, I believe your report also addresses the concept or the assertion that Croatian nationalists were the lineal successors of the Ustasha collaborators. Could you elaborate upon that concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it's been suggested that that was so. What the suggestion has been that what was being followed was the banovina plan of 1939. Now, that point has been made. Perhaps you'd like to comment on that, Mr. Almond.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think the agreement of 1939 was quite widely regarded by Croats as being the basis of an acceptable framework, that though because of the German invasion of Yugoslavia, it collapsed very quickly. The agreement between the constitutional parties of old royal Yugoslavia to redraw the administrative boundaries of the state in such a way that the vast majority of Croats lived within one territorial space, as I say, done under the constitutional arrangements of the kingdom of Yugoslavia, was something that a lot of Croats were nostalgic about, thought that would be a good, acceptable idea, because it was a political framework that had been based upon negotiation and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It was an acceptable framework based upon negotiation in the context of the constitutional arrangements of old Yugoslavia, royal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A portion of your report addresses stereotyping of Croats. Could you briefly summarise that.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in western Europe and also in the United States, going back into the 19th Century, Croats, as a nation, had been stereotyped as reactionaries, because in the conflicts, particularly surrounding the revolutions of 1848 to 1849, the Hungarian liberals were -- tended to be sympathised with by British/French/American liberal constitutionalists as being their natural allies. They seemed to be promoting a legislative framework based upon elections and so on that seemed broadly in line with what British, French liberals, constitutional proponents accepted. I think, myself, if we look at how the Hungarian liberals were also very nationalistic and how they treated the non-Hungarians within the territory of the kingdom of Hungary, which included Croatia, Vojvodina, and other parts of the former Yugoslavia at this time, then we can see that this was a misconception. But from that period in 1848, people from Karl Marx through to British liberals criticised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, I'm getting a request for you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. From 1848 a spectrum of opinion from liberals through to Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels attacked the Croats as reactionary because Croatian forces led by Ban Jelacic participated in the overthrow of the Hungarian revolution. Then in 1941, of course, the establishment of the so-called Independent State of Croatia, under the auspices of the German Nazi conquest of former Yugoslavia, revived and compounded that perception of the Croatians, as a nation, as being peculiarly reactionary. There is a particularly scholarly work from people like Edward Said and so on the notion of so-called Orientalism or the stereotyping of whole nations, particularly where those of us who come from fortunate countries, like Britain, where the constitutional and democratic and rule of law processes have not been interrupted, take a derogatory and often rather crude view of other nations. And I think that the Croatian case is an example of this. By contrast, for instance, the Serbs very frequently are classified as a nation, or at least were until perhaps 1999, as essentially natural allies of the West. They had fought in the First World War, and apparently in the Second World War, on the side of the West, and so had a good reputation to people who had not taken any close interest in the actual developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a historian, to what extent are those stereotypes significant in evaluating information relating to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: They don't necessarily help one to evaluate the conflict. What they help one to do is to evaluate how public policy, diplomats, personnel involved in the conflict from outside, may have come to the conflict with perceptions which were distorted by these stereotypes. And in my experience, these sorts of stereotypes were widely repeated in the training of British military personnel, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the Vance-Owen Plan and the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, can you elaborate upon what you describe as the device of the facts of those plans within communities?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The question of so-called cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a solution to the conflict was vitiated, I believe, particularly by the language used to describe those cantons, not least in public discourse, by Lord Owen, for instance, by his spokesman, whom I quote, John Mills, who tended to talk about them as ethnically controlled -- there would be Serbian, Croatian, or Muslim cantons -- and tended, for instance, to also describe the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as simply Muslim, which was, of course, what Belgrade and local Serb forces also said. So that the rhetoric associated with the peace plans actually, instead of calming the inter-ethnic tensions, confirmed them and I think even compounded them, because international statesmen seemed to confirm this way of looking at the conflict as legitimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a historian, would the various strains that you've described in your report and in your testimony be sufficient to explain the conflict between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats as opposed to a grand plan to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina by the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. I think the contingent events, these tragic and horrible events that had happened from the spring of 1992 in eastern Bosnia, then around Sarajevo and so on, had so destabilised and disrupted the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, even in areas not directly under the onslaught of the Bosnian Serbs, that this could easily explain, without any reference to what I regard as a chimerical conspiracy, how such tensions arise. And we only have to think of analogous conflicts, in Lebanon, for instance, where groups which start out being together find themselves falling out over resources, over accommodation, and so on, and the brutalising effects of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you address the theory or the claim that there was a plan at Karadjordjevo as being a statement that it was originated by opponents of President Tudjman. Could you explain that concept, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, I think although the fact of the meeting itself was known very early on, the main source, to my knowledge, for the claim that there had been a collusive agreement to dismember Bosnia-Herzegovina, against the wishes of its inhabitants and with brutal consequences, was made by Mr. Stipe Mesic, now president of Croatia. What is problematic about Mr. Mesic's claims is that, first of all, he wasn't present at the meeting. Secondly, he made these claims only after -- in public, at any rate -- only after he had quarrelled with President Tudjman and fallen from the high positions that he held in the government of Croatia and also in Mr. Tudjman's party. The main source from the Tudjman side, his principal private secretary advisor Sarinic gives an account of the meeting which is inconclusive, and that was published much more recently. Its precisely the subsequent developments, the conflict between Serbs and Croats, that makes me -- that convinces me that you have to believe in the most abstruse, sophisticated, and frankly absurd conspiracy theory to believe that there was a persistent pattern of collusion going back to that period, or at any date, and that in practice, in 1995, I think a lot of military historians and military analysts I've spoken to at the Pentagon recently would say that it was Croatian army's intervention that decisively reversed the Bosnian Serb conquests and brought about the conditions for the Dayton settlement, and that the NATO bombardment was an important factor, but without the Croatian army's role, that the defeat of the Bosnian Serbs and the establishment of the Dayton arrangements could not have arisen. I think that's the common view amongst military historians, military analysts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Almond. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, is there anything that you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite a good technique to avoid going to fast where we speak the same language, just put the headphones around your neck, turn them to channel 5 which is French, and if you turn the volume up sufficient to hear it as a background noise, it's then possible to know when we can start the next question or answer?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters, in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It took us months to work it out. Let me see if I understand where we are. So far as Dr. Donia's report is concerned, you may disagree with it as to certain nuances, but you're not saying that it's in any sense wholly and obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The thrust of his report with regard to the charge of a collusion between Croatia and -- certainly between the Croatian president and the Serbian president seems to me to be wholly wrong. In fact, Dr. Donia makes many points and quotes many facts and so on which are true, but I differ quite fundamentally on that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that, as the Judges have indicated, is ultimately a factual matter they've got to decide but insofar as historians can have a view on this sort of matter that is your principle disagreement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There are also some points of interpretation on the identity of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state or civic community. One of the problems is that, of course, many facts which one agrees on can nonetheless produce different conclusions. It's a common problem with historians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the Bosnia-Herzegovina interpretation, you're not suggesting that Dr. Donia's views are outside the spectrum of accepted modern academic --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: They're within the realm of debate, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As indeed is his conclusion on what you describe as the -- you don't describe as "the plan" but the plan and so on. That's, again, something well within the spectrum of respectable opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think that particularly I make the point in my report that many people who might, in other regards, agree with Dr. Donia's scholars, I quote Noel Malcolm and Ivo Banac and so on, of this particular point, suggests that it is an exaggeration to the point of distortion to suggest or -- conclusion so that they may be critical of Tudjman in other regards. They may be critical of the Croats in regard to the events of 1993, but that even scholars who, in other regards, would tend to agree with Dr. Donia do not agree with this thrust of argument that there was an underlying and continuous scheme of partition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Have you also read Dr. Allcock's report?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I've looked through it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looked through it. Just so I can understand it, is there any particular comment you want to make on that before you move on or are you happy to let that be dealt with by the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think the next witness is probably more competent to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the next witness, Mestrovic, we'll hear from him, of course, but part of what he seems to rely on is cultural irreconcilabilities between various parties and he seems to rely on a forthcoming conflict between Islam and the west. Do you think that's all terribly important?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: A lot of commentators, academics, politicians apparently from the public domain quoted [indiscernible] regard the threat of conflict with Islam very seriously. I, myself, though regarding such people as having serious interests on the subject perhaps think that it is less serious and it may be that some of the potential conflict is not entirely the product of Islam but also the product of western actions or perceptions of western actions and attitudes. But it doesn't seem to me to be inherently unreasonable to fear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where he forecasts -- not where he forecasts, where he relies on cultural differences between people in western Europe and people in Bosnia from whom much lower and lesser standards of performance could be expected, do you agree with him on that?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have to say, by the way, that I have not read his report. I know his academic work, so that it would be improper of me to comment on specific aspects of what the text says that I haven't read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing now with a few questions about your curriculum vitae. Did you type your report yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that when we look at the curriculum vitae, this is your own formulation of your academic background, the small correction you very helpfully made in relation to the 1986 entry is something I was going to ask you about, as His Honour Judge May will know and others may not, at Oxford, of course, you are a lecturer to the university and a fellow at a college. You are presumably a fellow at Oriel College?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I am a lecturer at Oriel College, a member of the history faculty, a member of the congregation. They are layers of status or rank; professor, who would also be a fellow of the college, a fellow, a lecturer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are not actually a fellow at Oriel nor at any other college?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are not a university lecturer?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No, I teach at the university. The university, as you may know, organises the supervision of graduate students, so when I supervise graduate students for higher degrees, that is organised by the University of Oxford. And then as a teacher of undergraduates, I teach at Oriel College, but may also teach and do from time to time undergraduates from other colleges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your lecturing is only with Oriel College.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No. The position is the position at Oriel College, but I teach, in addition to the Oriel students, students from other colleges as requested and as feasible within my --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. That's general policy of farming out work.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. And the graduate students, for instance, are organised by the university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you have no lectureship within the university itself?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No. But I think this may be a confusion of language. I say the position of university lecturer is a position in the academic hierarchy. I may have given lectures, seminars and so on in the university in the sense of addressing either students or gatherings of academics and anybody who cares to attend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't set out your formal qualifications. No doctorate is listed.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm mister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No doctorate is listed?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No, as I say, I'm mister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever started a doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes, I started my research on German intellectual history in the middle 19th century with particular reference to Richard Wagner and by extension to Chopin and if it is of assistance to the Court, how do I come to be interested in, particularly east European Balkan developments, part of archival and other research required for that took place in East Germany and I also visited Czechoslovakia. I became interested, as is not uncommon with young researchers, in those societies and, by connection, contacts I made in other societies in what was then called the socialist world. If I may be perhaps self-flattering. A well known historian in Oxford, Timothy Garton-Ashe, I think, in a sense, we followed the same path. He started to do research on German history, didn't complete a doctorate, has written extensively. Is a fellow of St. Anthony's College, Oxford, for instance, and has also, per chance, a visiting professor at the Hoover Institution. It's not an entirely uncommon phenomenon, no less common, perhaps, than in the past.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You started this doctorate when?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I started doing my research in -- after completion of my degree in 1980 and then was diverted into working on east European matters and teaching and writing about other matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now just to finish the questions I wanted to ask you on your curriculum vitae, of course, in England and particularly at Oxford, but in England in particular, the term "professor" is a very particular term noting, as it does, that leading of a department, holding of a chair and --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think actually -- certainly, it is a very distinguished title. In practice in Oxford, the professors, regis professor, for instance, or whatever do not actually run the department. The chairman of the department is elected by the members of the history faculty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And below the professor there might be the next rank down who might be a reader?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in America, a professor has a slightly more general term referring to those who teach, but when you cite yourself as a visiting professor at the Hoover Institution, is that accurate or would that perhaps be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, the Hoover Institution elected me to what they call, I'm afraid I did not use the title a "distinguished visiting professorship" which is a position to enable me to pursue the research project that had I proposed to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the proposed research is into the editorial policies and content of four influential American newspapers, isn't it, focussing on the impact of those newspapers on foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Amongst other issues, but particularly more and more focussing on foreign policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I was appointed last August, no, formally notified, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because isn't the reality that the title in Hoover has always been, so far as you're concerned, "distinguished visiting fellow" and the word professor has never been used to cover your work at all? Perhaps you'd like to look, please, at this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The commonplace -- certainly the members of the Hoover Institution you just referred to as fellows, if I have made a mistake, as I say, I have not wished to appeal to this authority except that in conversations on the telephone with people that have routinely referred to me as professor, so when drafting this curriculum vitae, if that is an error, I don't see it as altering the signification, but I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In America, there is a difference, again, between professor, which is to teach, and fellow, which may be to study, and you've got a grant to study, what, for one year?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sticking with your curriculum vitae, what is the date, please, of the first work published by you concerning Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I wrote a paper called the "Blundering in the Balkans".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a pamphlet effectively. And until then, you had written nothing about Yugoslavia because your interests had been elsewhere and in particular in Romania?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Romania is a neighbouring state of Yugoslavia and particularly in the late 1980s and after 1989, of course, Yugoslavia represented a fascinating comparison and counterexample with the collapse of the communist regimes like the neighbouring states of Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, of course, it was an opportunity for academics to work with a developing and unusual situation?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Because of what I had been studying before this period, I felt, first of all, that I was struck by the lack of interest in what seemed to me to be the potential of growing evidence of a likely violent conflict and by some of the assumptions about it that were disseminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been described by counsel as a historian. I put this question to you: A historian, I think you would accept, is somebody who works with raw material, the primary sources, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Those resources are available. I think that historians use all the available resources to them including, as it were, reflection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are, of course, in relation to the former Yugoslavia, considerable quantities of primary source material available, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: In almost every area of considerable quantity of resources with regard to the breakup of Yugoslavia and the reaction to it of the International Community especially the west European states and the United States, there are relatively few primary sources in the sense of publicly-available government documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't speak the language, I think.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I read it badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have -- having had some experience with -- I started to try to teach myself from 1991 and through the period and I regret that my abilities as a linguist are not greater than they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one, certainly an English speaker, will complain about limitations on linguistic ability, but the reality is that your publications on Yugoslavia, I think, cite no primary source material written in Croatian or B/C/S, do they?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I don't think that's entirely to the point. Most of what I've been writing about uses the sources in the languages of the international mediators or the foreign policy -- but there are my, as I say, torturous reading of my dictionary or whatever certain resources to confirm things, but I wouldn't claim to be, for instance, a cultural historian or literary historian of Serbo-Croatian; that would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the simple answer, correct me if I am wrong, is that neither in your earlier writings nor in your report for this Tribunal have you been able to or have you referred to any primary source material in Serbo-Croatian, to use its old title?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There may be a few instances, but the task of my report was to write about the perception of these events with particular relationship to the breakup of Yugoslavia and the international negotiations. I have, I think, cited one or two cases where I have checked sources to the best of my ability, limited ability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, for example, just to take one example, Tudjman, the historian, the books, are they translated into English for you to read or have they been, as it were, not available to you because they are in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I don't know how far all of President Tudjman's voluminous works have been translated. Many of them have been and many of them have been widely discussed in a scholarly literature. As well as I possess several of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You aren't able to turn to them when you want to check on the history of Tudjman's views on --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As I say, my reading knowledge is not as good as it should be, and I have occasionally checked because, of course, it's a matter of controversy and quite often in reviews of these works, individual words or whatever will be cited or discussed and debated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I think will be helpful and most efficient in our use of time is if I will go through your report with you asking a comparatively number of questions which I have to ask and which I have written marginal notes and stopping at particular topics in due course reviewing additional materials you've told us about this morning. So if you would be so good enough to take your report, please, and turn to the top right hand corner which is page three and in the fourth paragraph, you make an observation on statements by President Tudjman, decrying the perceived danger of Islamic fundamentalism, and you say that several SDA leaders have been educated radical Arab states. The next sentence: If we recall how many US commentators -- incidently I should pause, I trust that the interpreters have all got the report before them -- and even the CIA has warned about the potential influence of Islamic fundamentalists in Bosnia and other parts of the Balkans -- a fear that I regard as greatly exaggerated -- then Tudjman's attitude does not appear abnormal or particularly sinister. Do you think that it was then acceptable at the time and not in itself dangerous to be expressing what might be described as racist views about Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm not sure that these were racist views about Muslims quo Bosnian Muslims or racist in that they are about religious views. The -- particularly if we go back to the -- late 1980, 1990s with the Iranian revolution and the developments in Lebanon, it was a commonplace fear expressed, as I say, by western policy makers and statesmen as published from the CIA that there would be the penetration of radical Islamic ideology into the territories which had Muslim populations and one has to distinguish between the fear of a radical Muslim ideology radicalising people of Muslim origin and being against them as a group per se.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question still remains, if you would like to add to your answer, was it not dangerous given the composition of Bosnia, in the early 1990s, to express views adverse to an entire religious group represented in that state?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: To express that view might well be dangerous if that was the view expressed. Certainly it might be understood that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course -- sorry, it would -- it's danger would lie in the fact that it would whip up emotions nascent or even nonexistent in the minds of, in this case, Croats, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It might have that effect, but I think one has to remember that this was a fear expressed widely. As I say, I think myself, it was exaggerated and that, for instance, in so far as Iranian and other -- several Mujahedin influence has developed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would appear to be in reaction to the war, the Bosnian Serb onslaught and also perhaps to disappointment with the post-1995 settlement. It's not unknown for people to become more religious, who were quite secular, under the impact of terrible pressure and events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move from that point, one last question. The Chamber here has heard evidence that Mujahedin fighters, insofar as they are shown to have been taking part, either all or most had to cross Croatia to get to Bosnia, therefore had to be given passes, I suppose, to do so. How does that fit, in your judgement -- if that's what the Chamber finds, and these are all factual matters, of course -- how does that fit with Tudjman expressing genuine concerns about global developments as opposed to his simply having a rather more local ambition?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, I think it fits with a slightly different point, that the Croatian government, whatever its fears or whatever its resentment about previous attitudes on the part of Bosnia in the run-up to the war when itself was in war in 1991, permitted assistance to the Bosnian government's side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It certainly doesn't fit, does it, with, as it were, genuine concern about a forthcoming Islam Christian divide?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that it fits with a genuine fear, priority of fear, that the victory of the Bosnian Serbs presented a greater threat than any other threat, including an Islamic fundamentalist threat, to Croatia. It seems as though that if -- the line would be that Croatia was permitting assistance to go to Bosnia even from people that in other circumstances it might not be very happy about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go to page 4 next. The central paragraph reads as follows. Yes, I'm grateful. The point -- just to close that last discussion. The Mujahedin, on the evidence, came post-Graz, so does that affect your answer at all?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No. As I say, it seems -- I don't know whether -- you may want to ask me about Graz at another occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will do, yes. We'll come back to it, then. Page 4, the central paragraph: "Bosnian Croat preparations for self-defence take on a different appearance when it is remembered that President Izetbegovic's authorities had not attempted to inhibit the operations of the JNA from Bosnian territory against Croatia in 1991 and that they had cooperated with the JNA by ordering the Territorial Defence to hand in weapons to it." Then you say, "Such confidence-building measures failed to appease Belgrade." Isn't the reality at the time that both the Croats and the Muslims together were attempting to stall Milosevic's mobilisation of reservists?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: That is a different point. Many --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, isn't that correct, that all the --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I believe it to be correct that ordinary Muslims and Croats, and also people in positions of authority, did not wish them to go and fight against Croatia, but that several quite prominent officers in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina subsequently did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: But there are variations -- as I suggested, I think, earlier in my testimony, President Izetbegovic was very anxious to avoid a conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't blame him for that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this paragraph doesn't lead to any particularly significant conclusion, does it, as to what happened between Croats and Muslims in due course? At this stage they were pursuing a common line of resisting Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think one has to distinguish between resistance and a dislike of what Milosevic is doing. The Bosnian -- first of all, the number of Bosnian Croats, of course, went to Croatia to fight on the side of their fellow Croats in the army. The situation in the late summer, autumn and summer of 1991 was that it was not inconceivable that, and certainly it would be quite probable, that the policy of the Serbs was to split the Muslims from the Croats, and that evidence of what you call resistance as opposed to passive non-cooperation and unenthusiastic agreement to certain JNA demands on the part of the Bosnian government side, that there was therefore a split in the response of the Bosnian government side, for the sake of argument, the Muslims, and of the Bosnian Croats, who were aware of what was happening to their fellow Croats in Croatia and might reasonably fear that they would be the next target if such a war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which, for whatever reason, the Muslim community had been neutralised or had stood aside or taken -- perhaps even in some sense accepted continued Yugoslav authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to interrupt. It's just after 11.00. Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Mr. Almond, I must warn you, as I do all witnesses: Don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over and don't let anybody speak to you about it. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, I've a request from the court reporters; if you would speak slowly and distinctly, they would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I mumble in any language I know or don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last point on the mobilisation issue, which you had dealt with at page 4. Now, I'm going to come back to the sources available to you in particular in a minute, but who do you say it was who decided against mobilisation? Who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As I understand it -- you mean mobilisation to oppose the JNA's activities with regard to the war going on in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As I understand it, the government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the government in Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic and his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, it's quite important to be precise on these matters, isn't it? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you mean President Izetbegovic or do you mean the presidency? Who was it who made that non-mobilisation decision, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It would have been made under the authority of the presidency, but I haven't got the exact document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course you will have read, no doubt, Susan Woodward's book -- that's in English -- Balkan Tragedy, and she sets out quite clearly at page 260 that it was the presidency that made that order. So the presidency, of course, included Croat members, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that your paragraph here, where you say, "where it is remembered that President Izetbegovic's authorities," and so on, do you think that's being entirely fair?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, as I said first of all earlier on, I didn't mean necessarily that one should impugn the intentions or the desire to avoid conflict on the part of either President Izetbegovic or members of his party or people who cooperated with him in Sarajevo. But if we look at the context, I think there is a lot of evidence that people in the predominantly Croatian areas, the activists who were sympathetic to the cause of Croatia which was at war, felt that perhaps the government in Sarajevo, including even Croat members of it, were not aware of -- or not fully aware of the threat that they believed the JNA posed. I think, for instance --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm going to cut you off, because we don't have, unfortunately, limitless time. My question to you simply is this: In your expert report, do you think focusing on President Izetbegovic, when the available material to you showed that this was a decision of the presidency that included Croats, do you think that was entirely fair in your report, or should we really think that this ought to be slightly revised?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It may be slightly revised to take into account that people who were of Croatian origin in the presidency who were participants in these decisions, but I'm not sure that taking all the evidence available to me from the sources that I have, ranging from the sort of books that you quote through to the summaries, the BBC summaries of world broadcasts and FBIS and so on, that one wouldn't find that if we look at the perception, certainly, the perception of many Bosnian Croats was that the initiative for this was primarily one for the sake of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate that further with you. Before I come to the next major topic and the only one that's going to take any significant -- a great period of time, just back again to your function. As you've told us, I think, you were dealing with available English predominant sources in order to give perceptions or give an account of the perceptions outside Bosnia of what was happening within. Now, if that's right, how does that enable you to express opinions on what was happening at Karadjordjevo and so on?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that any of the so-called expert witnesses were present at the event. The discussions of Karadjordjevo have been widely discussions promoted by claims about what happened by, for instance, Mr. Mesic, have been widely distributed in various languages and are available. My point was that one doesn't have to impugn the honesty of the motives of people who believe, I believe, mistakenly in a collusive, persistent pattern of collusion between Zagreb and Belgrade to see that from what I would normally regard as the commonly accepted record of events. It is very difficult to interpret this process of conflict and the disintegration of Yugoslavia in that way. And, for instance, if I may direct one source which is available of one of the people who was a participant, Sarinic, if you like who was the closest advisor to President Tudjman, he makes the point to August 1995 that there was a telephone conversation with Milosevic. Milosevic complains that the Croatian army is serving, is destroying the Bosnian Serb position, is creating the disaster of the Bosnian Serbs and why is Tudjman pushing through such an aggressive policy which is only going to help the Muslims. In other words, that Tudjman is not pursuing a purely Croatian policy, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if we go back, you see, if I may say so, the beginning of this long answer, you make the point --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you press "transcript" on your button, the English transcript will come before you. You make it plain that you believe it to be a mistake that there was any pattern of collusion. You are prepared to express an opinion on what happened at this meeting. Let's just deal with your answer. The man, Sarinic, has written a book but it's in Croatian, of course, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It is in Croatian. I happen to have a copy of it in Croatian and I also have --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you managed to read all of it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I haven't read the whole of it in Croatian. I have checked partly with the Croatian text some of the translations which have made by various services, but I primarily read what I know of it in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the passage in that book where Sarinic refers to a conversation that he and Tudjman had flying over Bolovocelo [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Do you have the text in front of you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think I have it. I didn't know you were going to mention it just then. I just wondered if you remembered that particular passage, perhaps you don't.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now aware that there's now been a book published by Milos Milic which puts together either all or a very great amount of the evidence about the Karadjordjevo meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I've not seen it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, it's not in English but you haven't even seen it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some of the material that might have been available to you, but before we do, remind me, I may have made a note and I'm sorry if I'm asking you to repeat yourself, but remind me, what do you say happened, in your opinion, at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: In my opinion, there was a discussion between the two presidents, Milosevic of Serbia and Tudjman of Croatia, about if Yugoslavia was going to disappear, which was certainly a reasonable prospect, what would succeed it? Part of the tragedy, particularly of the Bosnian Muslims but of the whole population of Bosnia-Hercegovina was, of course, that it was not a republic with a homogenous population as of Slovenia or a large majority of individual group of population as perhaps in Croatia or in Serbia. So that a discussion about what would happen to the Serbs of Serbia, Serbs of Bosnia, I should say, and the Croats of Bosnia and how that might be, as a result, I think, undoubtedly took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no question of annexation?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It depends how -- what you mean by "annexation". I don't -- presumably if two sovereign states, Serbia and Croatia, were created, and Bosnia-Herzegovina either did not become a fully sovereign state or was divided, not necessarily solely between the two states, then part of it would have passed to each of those republics. I do not know whether, as I say, the -- it seems to me that discussion may have taken place, but whether there was planning and certainly whether there was agreement, I find the subsequent developments made highly implausible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no reason, therefore, to discuss, especially in the absence of a representative in the Muslim community, any partition of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, if I personally think that the dissolution of Bosnia-Herzegovina could have been vastly better arranged, I don't think that anybody would have said that the developments of 1991 were beneficial, in fact, even to the Serbs let alone to Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the question is that we're looking at your opinions. You've given your opinion and we've got to try to evaluate it.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, would there be any way that these two men could have been discussing a tripartite or bipartite division of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It seems perfectly possible at that meeting and certainly, in my view, likely that the idea that Bosnia-Herzegovina would not become an independent, republic, sovereign state in its boundaries as established under Yugoslav constitution was absolutely part of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you deal with the question. Would there be any grounds then without the Muslims present to be discussing partition, whether into two or into three?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: If a plan had been formulated and adopted and acted upon to divide another republic without consultation, that would be, I think, a different matter ethically irreprehensible from a discussion about a discussion about what might -- and my understanding is that this is a discussion about what might have been. As you know, I think, from things that I've published in the past, my own personal preference would have been for a Bosnian-Herzegovinian republic, but I'm not sure in this state of flux between the effective collapse of the monopoly of the Yugoslav League of Communists which had held federal Yugoslavia together and the outbreak of conflict, it is necessarily evidence of criminal intent to discuss alterations to the internal boundaries which subsequently the International Community chose to recognise as the boundaries of sovereign states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an English reader you would have, of course, count as your sources, English newspaper articles, English television programmes?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Among them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you are presumably familiar with a comparatively recent, was it 1995, 1994, sorry, dispatches programme that dealt with this particular meeting containing some eyewitness account of it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember, there are so many of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it, Exhibit 1682, please. If you push the second button down.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: "Video evidence"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Video", I think, the top one, you'll get it.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is plainly material that you perhaps should be aware of. Had you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think in retrospect I did see the programme, yes. On the point -- I don't -- there were two points, if I may make, I'll come back to the second in a second. The actual contents are broadly similar to what I have suggested there were these discussions including possible partition, possibly into three parts, I think I said, but that came to no active conclusion.
