On the second point, the programme itself -- with music and also the pictures of the two presidents with their wine creates an impression which you could for instance show pictures of Richard Halbrooke or Lord Owen in the same context and dramatise it so on the content --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure I can cut you short, the drama isn't going to affect the Judges. It's what the two witnesses Bilandzic and Letica say. It's not people who you've turned --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: But I know Letica is a well-known figure in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are not people to whom you've turned to for assistance?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Not directly. I have seen interviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They make it quite plain that there was an official denial, that means a denial, including to the Muslims of the content of these talks. Why, if it was just concerned with the ultimate security and safety and future of this state, can you think of any reason why there should be just bilateral talks to the exclusion of the third party, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Precisely because the Serb leadership had already made various claims to territory in Croatia and in Bosnia which was in their view either wholly or predominantly inhabited by Serbs. There was a question of how to avoid a conflict. I have made the point already that I don't believe that contacts between Bosnian Muslims and the Serb authorities are necessarily to be seen as reprehensible because they sought to avoid conflict. I think the relations between Tudjman and Milosevic were also not inherently reprehensible and I'm not sure -- clearly apart from anything else, I think if one looks at many international discussions including between leaders who are universally accepted as democratic and legitimate, they often involve denials of what has been discussed because they do not wish to be embarrassed over points which are not necessarily going -- criminal or conspiratorial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to the question once and then move on to the next piece of evidence. Can you think of any reason why, if they were deciding on the future of this state generally, they were bilateral and why the Muslims were excluded, any good reason?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. In the context of violence by Serbs in Croatia and the need to, from the point of view of the Croatian government, to calm that conflict and also the need to avoid further conflicts, Tudjman had to talk to somebody who was already widely regarded as Milosevic as deeply reprehensible and unpopular. It would be very foolish of any diplomat, I would suggest, to put all his cards straight on the table. There were, after all, alternatives being discussed and it seems to me that these alternatives, which are not ones that I would necessarily or need -- not ones that I would support, nonetheless were part of a broader picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, two points emerge from that, since you raise that as an answer. I'm sorry I'm making a mistake of not leaving a gap. The first point is this, if that was Tudjman's motivation then he should, of course, immediately have gone and discussed things with Izetbegovic explaining what he was doing in the general interest, shouldn't he? And there is no evidence that he ever did.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: That might have been wiser, but it would have been, of course, essential if an agreement had been reached, but your own television interviews suggest that options were discussed not an agreement made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a short step -- sorry. My mistake again. It is a short step from any discussion about partition to consideration of annexation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then now please look at the next piece of evidence that you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you move on, I wanted to ask Mr. Almond this general question. What impact does your conclusion that there was no plan between Croatia and Serbia to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina have on how one looks at the actual conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I see that conflict as being more produced by contingent events in -- after the war breaks out in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, and not the product of a conscious plan by the Croatian government to promote a conflict between Muslims and Serbs, for instance. I have not seen any evidence of that. And as I suggested in response to an earlier question, I think -- I'm not obviously competent, as I'm sure the Prosecution would agree, to comment on the specific events in question with regard to who murdered whom and why in April 1993. But if we look at the context of how this conflict arose, it seems to me that to isolate it from the Serb Muslim conflict and also from the general conflicts that have broken out from June 1991, and in the case of Croatia, even with the quasi-secession of Krajina from August 1990, to isolate the conflicts that broke out in Central Bosnia from that context, I feel -- I believe to be misleading. It is perhaps comforting to feel that there was a structure, a nice neat pattern leading to that conflict. I feel myself that it is a tragic consequence of the Bosnian Serb onslaught against, in this case, primarily the Bosnian Muslims, and how that interacts with the territory that they're pushed into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before I part from what you've just been saying, in a sentence, the conflict emerges because it's produced by contingent events after the war breaks out. I want to come back to this. But that's your analysis: Produced by contingent events after the war breaks out?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, please, look at Exhibit 2717, if the witness could have that. And it's an English document, so I think because the Judges don't have their own copies and it's quite a large document, it will be helpful if we simply lay it on the ELMO and look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to go through various passages of this document and tell me how you say it fits with your theory. It's a document with which you're familiar. It's the record of the meeting on the 27th of December of 1991 in Tudjman's office. So if we look at page -- and I'm going to deal with the content of the meeting by topics. If we look at page 8, please. Can I take it, Mr. Almond, that you have in fact looked at and considered the totality of this document?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which case, I'll deal with passages shortly. If you believe that there's a question of context, I'd ask you to tell me. On page 8, we see the president interrupting Kljuic, saying, "Tell me, in these talks about partition, did you get to the heart of the matter?" Kljuic says, "No. They would not commit themselves. We were trying to take them at their word." And then at the top of the next page the president says, "No. It is about partition." If we look at page 21, this is the president speaking, and a long passage. And two lines, three lines down from the top, he says this, as one of the arising questions: "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent internationally recognised Croatia ..."

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a different text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's higher on the page. Sorry. Right at the top of the page. There we go. Two lines down from the top. "It seems to me, therefore, that just as we have taken advantage of this historic moment to establish an independent internationally recognised Croatia, I believe that it is time that we take the opportunity to gather the Croatian people inside the widest possible borders." And then at the bottom of the same page, after an intervention by Mr. Boban or, a contribution by Mr. Boban: "Let me finish," says the president, "so the discussion can go on. It seems to me, therefore, that with a prudent policy, a clever demarcation and agreement with the Serbs in Bosnia, we can even achieve that instead of war, which is threatening, because of this unresolved issue, the army buildup, that the army will serve as a guarantee for the implementation of such a demarcation." Before I look at the next passages, do none of these passages even suggest to you that Tudjman had partition and annexation in mind?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It seems, for instance, from the passage you've just quoted, that there was no agreement with the Serbs. That's one point. That he thinks that if the agreement with the Serbs could be achieved -- and we are, of course, talking still at a time when it is not clear that Bosnia-Herzegovina will become an independent state --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: Did he --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry on. Did he not have partition and annexation in mind? What's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: A partition was a possibility that had been discussed or was widely touted, because I think a point of common agreement amongst the various people who have been asked to testify on the aspects of whether Croatia regarded -- Croats, sorry, regarded Croats abroad as being foreigners, of course there was this dilemma. People had lived in a common state for a long time. If you were to create borders between them, would you divide populations who had lived together? And we have to remember that the armed conflict in Croatia itself was, to put it at best, on ice at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we look at page 55, over to 56, just picking it up for context at the foot of 55. At the bottom of 55, he asks -- the president asks if anybody else wants to speak. And it says that the discussion has shown that this meeting is not necessary -- was necessary and that differences surfacing are not accidental, conditioned by the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself. And then over to page 56, he says: "All of history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is no solution for the Croatian people. First of all, gentlemen, let us not forget that it, Bosnia, was created in the colonial conquest of an Asian power at the expense of the Croatian people and Croatian territories between the 15th and 18th centuries. All colonial creations throughout history fell, both in Africa and Asia. Bosnia and Herzegovina did not exist between the two world wars. The communists invented it, put it back on the map after World War II, even declared the Muslims to be a nation, in order to supposedly resolve the differences between the Serbian and Croatian people. Did they succeed? No. On the contrary. Therefore, Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be taken as something God-given, which must be preserved, and we must especially not forget how harmful it is." What do you say to that passage?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think if you read the next paragraph, you can see that he makes the point that the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina creates what he calls an impossible situation with regard -- regarding its territory, regarding administration, not to mention defence: "We cannot establish an independent Croatia such as it is." Part of the problem of anybody looking at the map would be to say that the territorial shape of Croatia is problematic in all sorts of aspects, and particularly, as I say, in this context where we have had the war with Serbia which has made use of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely so, Mr. Almond. What the president was saying was, "We need a chunk of Bosnia to make ourselves more viable," simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's quite so simple as that at all. If we look at the various proposals at different times, the Croatian leadership had talked as though the integration of the Croats into Bosnia was the only solution because of the war situation. At other times they looked to a common state. I remember, for instance, discussing with Muhamed Sacirbeg the various times -- the Bosnian government ambassador to the United Nations, at a conference in Crans, Montana in 1996, and he made a point which was that the Croats had proposed various integrations between Bosnia and Croatia which would render -- would, for instance, have a common currency. He took the view, as I remember him, that this would of course mean that there would be complete integration of the two states. Whether that is necessarily malign is a different point. On your -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just look over at page 57, because we want to deal with it as swiftly as we can while giving you a chance to comment on all the passages that I'm going to suggest to you show your theory to be wholly groundless. Page 57, about eight lines up from the bottom, but start at a fresh paragraph. The president is still speaking. "The Croatian Democratic Union ..." Shall we put it on the ELMO? "The Croatian Democratic Union and the state leadership of Croatia have not changed. There have been no changes. No. But because we -- I shall not repeat what all you said -- we said that for tactical reasons we were in favour of a sovereign Bosnia, so long as it existed, but there is no longer a sovereign Bosnia." What does that say to you, please, Mr. Almond, about partition being in the president's mind, and annexation?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, he carries on to say, "The Serbs have split off. You have no authority. The Bosnian government has no authority over the Serbian sections." And above the paragraph you quote, I believe he makes the point that he has spoken with Izetbegovic in private talks with Milosevic, in talks with both of them. There was discussion of how to find a solution -- such a solution which would satisfy both the Croatian and Serbian people as well as the Muslims. It was discussed. So I think the picture in the document that you cite, or the Prosecution cites, is somewhat more complex, and particularly if we remember this point, which seems to come out of the direct citations you make, that the authority of the government in Sarajevo over the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was collapsing. Until this stage -- and there are many more lawyers. Although I'm not a lawyer, there are lawyers here. Usually in international law the British government would recognise the government only if it controlled the territory of its state. That may have changed after the event, but not at this time, and therefore I think the connotation you put upon these words, particularly taken away from the context on either side, makes them more aggressive than in fact they need to be seen as.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Surely, surely, Mr. Almond, the words I've read out to you, and I'm happy that you put them in their context indeed, the words make it quite clear that whatever was being said in public in favour of a sovereign Bosnia no longer applied and Tudjman had a different object in mind, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think Tudjman was not in charge of events, so that observing the developments, the hope, which it seems implicit in what he says, that a sovereign Bosnia breaking away from Yugoslavia would not therefore be a launching pad for Serbian power, also vis-a-vis Croatia, that at this stage in late December no longer seems to be viable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last on this topic and this run-through of the document, although I shall take you to some other pages, page 66. The whole of what the president says in this short passage, so that there's context: "That is what it's about. Therefore, what is being said in some circles, that they created Herceg-Bosna of their own will, or at my instructions, is not true. It is not true. They and you both, and each in a somewhat one-sided way, without sufficient coordination, implemented the general policy, and the general policy was to preserve sovereignty until a certain moment so long as it was convenient for Croatia. Now it is no longer convenient. So what they did is exactly what you are saying. The Croats do not want to join Serboslavia; therefore, this is the road we need to take to achieve a Croatian state which will be better in every respect." Can you fit that to anything other than a clear expression of intent to take some of the spoils of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It seems to me to be making the point that Serboslavia, which was a common term for the idea of a continued Belgrade-dominated state led presumably by Mr. Milosevic, was something that Croats would not wish to join, and therefore, in the context of the apparent imminent breakdown of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republic and its unlikelihood of it becoming a sovereign state, that those parts which were predominantly inhabited by Croats would naturally, in his view, wish to join Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at last, you accept that there is in his mind the question of parts of Bosnia being linked to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I make the point that if the choice is between a Bosnian-Herzegovinian republic that remains part of a Yugoslav state dominated, after all, politically and militarily by the people who have just attacked Dubrovnik and Vukovar, it would not be either desirable or acceptable to the Croats there, or to Croats in general, that that state should come about, because a glance at the map would show that the threat to the remaining -- the independence of the remaining Croatian states, 30 per cent approximately, occupied by Serbs, would be mortal. I think that Serboslavia in this context is a very important term. It is not, after all, saying they don't want to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now accepting that it is clear that the possibility of a bit of Bosnia joining Croatia is under discussion?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: In the context of the collapse of Bosnia-Herzegovina into -- under the control of the still existing Yugoslav state which I think that is, I imagine, what he meant by Serboslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you first set out in writing your acknowledgment that this form of annexation was first considered in your writing or in your report?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it's a form of annexation in that my understanding of this potential process is that the inhabitants, the Croatia inhabitants primarily of Bosnia-Herzegovina would not wish to live -- would not wish to live in such a state and would seek the obvious protection of their obvious protector which would be Croatia. He takes that for granted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer to my question, please -- reformulate the question as you like -- where in your writings do you ever acknowledge that there was going to be joinder or that there might have been joinder of part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia? First of all, is it in your report?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It's not explicitly in the report, because the report deals with the relevant sections of why there were tensions between Croats -- why Croats might fear the preservation of a Yugoslav state, even a diminishing one containing Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've read all this document which I've taken you through, or some bits of it. It's clear that however we use the word "annexation" or "joinder" was being considered, you've now given an explanation for how that comes about in the discussions. Didn't you think it important, given your divergence from Dr. Donia's views, to give your full understanding of how these topics came to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, I presume, for instance, that this document was available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the Court is prepared to accept or listen to your opinions on these matters, for that's the reason you're here.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: But I -- given --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I take it, and we'll move on, that nowhere in writing have you ever recorded your opinion that there could have been the joinder of part of Bosnia to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm not certain that I've never discussed, either in writing or in some verbal interview, that this prospect, at various times, might have been discussed. I think that's perfectly possible. But my key point is: I was asked specifically with regard to the allegation that from Karadjordjevo onwards there was a consistent policy, and it seems to me that even the document that you cite at length shows that this is a discussion in the dilemma in the late part of 1991, when the war between Serbia and Croatia had not stopped and the establishment of a sovereign independent Bosnia-Herzegovina is still, by no means, clearly going to take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've taken into account, have you, that this was five days after the presidency had decided to seek independence?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: But I think further back in this document, you will see, one of the participants in the meeting nonetheless says he doesn't really believe they will. You yourself have drawn attention, or the Prosecution has drawn attention, to the disparity between public statements and private intentions. And I'm afraid if we also remember the international context, it was not at all clear that either the European Community states, and certainly not the United States, would necessarily recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. The lack of such recognition which was not, as I say, at all clear would mean that the viability of the republic as a state would be even more in question, sadly, than it was because of the operations of the Bosnian Serb forces already in development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to stick with the immediate topic, with one more piece of evidence. And I may come back to that document, so we won't take it away for the time being. No doubt one of your sources of information is what's said in these trials.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have read some press reports, but apart from looking up Dr. Donia's contribution, which I've subsequently received in text form, I haven't had access to the transcripts of the trial, so it -- my sources are press reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Some of the events in these trials have gained a little publicity, and perhaps now the witness could see Exhibit 2486. You will remember, probably while it's coming to you, that evidence has been given by Paddy Ashdown about his banquet on the 6th of May, and this is straight from the hand of Tudjman and it's about as clear a diagram as you could have. The next page, please, the page that conveniently dates the banquet at which he drew this diagram, and if you'll look at it. Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: In the press, I think The Times published it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at it, because it's not entirely straightforward. The present Bosnia-Herzegovina border, obviously very much an approximation, has the lines with the criss-crosses around it, and the future Serbian-Croatian border, an "S" shape, is revealed, as are the present front lines and Sarajevo. Simple case of annexation even more generous to Croatia than the banovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The territorial division on this very approximate map might be, but I disagree with your argument simple case of annexation, because we would need to know the explanation given for the map. And if I may draw the attention of the Court to the context, in May of 1995 the Bosnian Serb forces seemed to be in an even stronger strategic position than they had been before. The elimination, which I regard in whole the prospect, but it was a prospect that the remaining territory controlled by the Bosnian government in Sarajevo would be overrun. As you will remember, in July of 1995, Zepce, Srebrenica were overrun with generally accepted horrific consequences. Therefore, the designation of this very approximate territorial division seems to me to indicate possibly, since I wasn't present at the conversation, unless you have evidence of what was said, that Tudjman may have been already envisaging his military operations which took place to reverse the Serb control of Krajina and Slavonia, and ultimately his intervention on the side of the Bosnian government in the context where it seems the International Community, despite its recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had abandoned it to its fate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you haven't actually considered what Mr. Ashdown had said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There were certain press reports of what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel. Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say -- you're making your opinions, you see, on the basis of sources available to you. Here is as close a source to Tudjman's mind as you can get.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid the force --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, some of that testimony was given in closed session, and that should be borne in mind as the answer to this question is being given.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The source has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we are assisted, Mr. Nice, by the witness' comments on what -- or his recollection of what Mr. Ashdown may or may not have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point of the matter is that we have the evidence of Mr. Ashdown in transcript form and we've had -- we've got the plan, and we've got the witness' comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move then, without prejudice, to the fact that I may come back to the meeting in December 1991 to Graz. Just tell us, please: What do you know about that, so you can tell us what your understanding is?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I -- as I understand it, Boban and Karadzic met and had discussions, which do not seem to have reached an agreement, on the future shape of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what, if anything, did they agree on?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your approach, or am I wrong, doesn't really allow for there to be any bilateral agreements between Serbia and Croatia at that time, does it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, these are not between Serbia and Croatia but between Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats, but also that there were contacts, either direct meetings or telephonic contacts, between various leaders, including the Bosnian government side and opponents, I think, is generally accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But please stick with the question. Your approach, your analysis of events doesn't really allow for any concluded agreements, secret or otherwise, between Bosnian Serbs and Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It doesn't allow for the implementation and consistent collaboration, because I do not believe that took place, and I believe the evidence on the ground suggests that that didn't take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 92.1, please, Exhibit 92.1. This starts off next -- well, it starts off with a fax message to Sarajevo all within the monitoring mission, and we go on to the next page from Cutilliero to a colleague Colm: "Could you, in your conference capacity, try to elucidate with the principals the exact terms and meaning of their alleged agreement and Muslim views on the matter? We have not been able to speak on the telephone for a few days. Warmest congratulations on your work from Lord Carrington and from me." And the next page is dated the 7th of May and says: "Boban and Karadzic have reached an agreement at a meeting concerning the resolution of all the differences between the two nations through conciliatory means, including the territorial delimitation under the auspices of the European Community. They reassured firmly the agreement of the principles defined in the conference in Lisbon. There is no further reason for the continuation of armed conflicts between the Serbs and the Croats. The territorial delimitation between the nations will be made until the 15th of May. Cease-fire will be decreed from today." And if you turn over, please, the next page is the agreement: "Our intention being to resolve peacefully, and by agreement, all outstanding issues, including the border line between our two constituent units." Then to save time, (1) is the Neretva River in Mostar; (2), the area delineated in 1939; (3), both sides agree that in defining the border line between the two units, accounts should be taken of compactness of areas; (4), both sides resolved in their adherence to the principles adopted in the conference; (5), the agreement makes invalid the reasons for the suspension of the EC conference, insists that the demarcation under arbitration be implemented by agreed-upon date of May 15th; (6), in view of the agreement outline above, no more reasons obtained for an armed conflict between the Croatians and the Serbs in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Obviously not a document you've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, I made -- in the answer to the previous question, the point I was making was that were these agreements implemented and carried out. You see, you have raised -- or the Prosecution raises a different point. An agreement, to me, and if this can clarify it, means something that is implemented. Was the -- this agreement implemented? Was it persistently abided by?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try and find my question. I can't deal with it -- the machine is too complicated -- but I think I asked you quite specifically: Was there any ground for these people making this agreement? Is this not an agreement that's been made?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It was the document side of an agreement, but it was an agreement, if I remember correctly, that was a dead duck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not an agreement which you had any recollection when I asked you about it.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have not read the -- I have not recollected the details of the text with, as you say, the specific points about the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I had seen a report of the agreement. I didn't say I had seen this direct text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go over, just again, to save time -- the two sheets are headed "Press Release." At a meeting late on -- this comes from just a press release, Ian Greer Associates.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "At a meeting late Wednesday in the town of Graz, the leader of the Bosnian Serbian Democratic Party, Mr. Karadzic, signed a peace agreement." It goes on to set out "with cease-fire," and so on. This was a well-reported -- or a report, in any event, concluded agreement. What does that tell you about the attitude of the Croats to the Bosnian Muslims at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Part of the agreement which you yourself created is the adherence to the European Community principles, and even Mr. Greer's press statement refers to three separate states, or, in other words, implicitly not a clear partition between Serbs and Croats. I haven't, of course, seen Mr. Greer's press release before. Mr. Greer, of course, a figure of some controversy because of his activities as a public relations consultant, but only for the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't show you these documents in English because we've only just obtained them and they aren't yet translated, I'm afraid, but you're aware, aren't you, that Zagreb is turning over quite a lot of documents at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm aware of press reports about this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there are documents in due course, and in 1993 from a man called Rajic in Kiseljak, making it absolutely clear that he is negotiating directly with the Serbs over the supply of the weapons with even a price list, what do you say about that? How does that fit with your overall theories?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As you say, I haven't had the opportunity to see these documents and I would not comment. I think in my book I make the point that war is very corrupt, and you will find examples on all sides of cross-conflict cooperation, sadly, and not just in this war, but without these documents are completely unknown to me, you -- the source of them, the verification of them, is something which I know nothing, so it would be very foolish to waste the time of the Court to comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you to, in any event, because they are documents, as we understand it, that have been provided by Zagreb to the Defence and the Prosecution and, in fact, to all parties. They will therefore be understood by the native speakers in the Defence, even though they have to be translated for some of those working on the Prosecution. The Judges may, in due course, see them and they may or may not make their mind up. But if, in 1993, we find Rajic in Kiseljak negotiating directly with the Serbs over the supply of weapons, what does that do to your theory, please? Does it harm it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I have no knowledge of these documents. That individual's -- clearly the whole point of this trial is that somebody did dastardly things. But for me to comment on these documents whose, as I say, selection and provision is something and authenticity is something about which I know nothing, would be, I think, wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In addition, Your Honour, if I may object. We haven't received any such documents along the line that the Prosecution is talking about, and I don't think it's right to put propositions based upon documents which may or may not exist and certainly which have not been translated yet and not been provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my plan is to ask a few more questions before 1.00. I'll then regroup, tidy up, and deal with the outstanding matters as quickly as I can after the break. I've discussed with Mr. Sayers the next witness can probably be taken in chief this afternoon, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, there is a problem about these documents which nobody's seen which are not in the language of the Tribunal, and normally, of course, one would want a document to be in the language of the Tribunal before a witness is invited to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And also, the other side should have a copy of it. So unless the circumstances are exceptional, the better way for dealing with it would be for the matter to be dealt with by way of rebuttal evidence, unless there's a particular point for a witness, in which case, of course, you can apply to the Court for leave to put it to him. But I think it would be better for you, in future, to apply for leave so we can have it discussed first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And my concern, of course, is to give the expert witnesses, in particular, an opportunity to comment on documents if it's helpful for them to do so, but there it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I come --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what remains before the lunch adjournment, can you please take your report and go to page 31. You say in this paragraph, in this page, on the penultimate paragraph: "It has been alleged that the interpreters," plural --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: This is page 31?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thirty-one of your report.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "... that the interpreters and local personnel employed by BritBat, as well as other international agencies and NGOs in the area, came predominantly from a Muslim background. Emotional entanglements between male officers and female locally employed staff from one group could well have distorted perceptions of developments." Is that seriously your proposition?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. I think the House of Commons Defence Committee has reported inter alia on the so-called problem of overstretch, and it has said that one of the problems for the British army, both in recruiting and retaining people, is caused by long periods of separation from families, the breakdown of marriage. That is one aspect of it. Secondly, it is a general problem, not so -- I'm not suggesting that this is some peculiar vice or flaw of members of BritBat, but it is an observable, sociological phenomenon of deployment in foreign territories abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're seriously suggesting, are you, that the whole reporting of this war by professional soldiers, whatever their consistency, before this Tribunal may have been infected by their emotional entanglements?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting their whole reporting, because, as you will have read, I make the point that other aspects of the briefing material that, as far as I know, was provided to them, would tend to encourage them to take a more hostile view of the Croats than of the Muslims. I made the point that, for instance, I addressed -- I had a lecture at the staff college at Camberley, and the nature of the questions and the comments was suggestive to me of people who had, since they had no necessary reason to be interested in the area, apart from what they were being trained to be deployed, that part of the problem was that there was a bias against the Croats, and secondarily. So these sorts of problems might encourage. But the perception -- you see, I think the great problem is people can be honestly biased. There are two types of bias, if you like. There is somebody who is deliberately making a propagandistic point, and then there are people who honestly believe what they believe but may be mistaken, and that certain factors go together to create their perceptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you -- just help us with this, from your -- was it a single briefing at Camberley? How were you able to say that that was, however unintentionally, biased? In what way was it biased? How are you right and they wrong?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Because the expression -- I mentioned earlier in answer to a previous question the kind of attitudes towards the Croats, weren't they all fascist during the war and so on, asking about the historical context, suggested to me that that was the kind of assumption that was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, so that we can have chapter and verse and, if necessary, explore it. Who was saying this?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There were both -- I gave a talk, there were questions and answers, and also there were brief private conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave a talk and were able to put the record straight to those who asked you questions that were, in a sense, ill-conceived, if they were.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. Whether I put the record straight is obviously a matter of judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to the interpreters, because you've used plural, who are these interpreters? What's their names? Who are the officers whose perception may have been affected?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we are going to be discussing a topic like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't -- can you speak more clearly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: If a matter such as this is going to be probed by Mr. Nice, perhaps it would make sense to go into closed session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: To the extent that he's asked specifics about specific individuals, specific British officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can't see there's any embarrassment about that, unless the witness feels it -- if the witness thinks that it's an embarrassing matter, of course we'll consider it, but it doesn't seem to me that it's immediately a matter for a private session. But Mr. Almond, can you answer the question or not?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: In the press reports about this matter, in, for instance, the so-called documentary drama broadcast by the BBC Warriors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's Warriors.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No, it isn't. There are widely reported -- I am also, as the Prosecution has pointed out, because I too use interpreters and observe people using interpreters, not only in the former Yugoslavia but in other places, that there is simply a professional difficulty that arises of objectivity. And that seems to me to be reasonable without going into the question of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've taken this as far as we can. Anything more on this topic, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not at that particular topic, no. That's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, I think it's a reality, is it not, that you have very strong views of your own regardless of your views on current affairs that you analyse, but you have strong views of your own about, for example, British involvement in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have views of my own, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, I suspect, think that it was entirely wrong for the British to be led into what they did via the European union; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Few people, I think, today, would say that the consequences were beneficial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I think --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: So I think it was wrong to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite specifically, you are against the British involvement with the European union, for example.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: In Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think that Britain, of course, played a leading role and the policies were mistaken, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You now, I think, take firmly the view that Croatia is unwise in selling itself out to the European union; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think the -- whether this is relevant to the case in hand along with other applicants state during the European union the conditions required to be met create a great deal of economic hardship and are not advantageous to the populations of almost all the applicant states, if this is relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also take the view personally, and I'm simply putting, as you would probably guess, some of the comments that you think you made earlier this year with Hrvatska Sloba in April?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also take the view that with the demise of communism, the west has become a less tolerant and liberal place and that there's some preponderance of socialist mentality permeating Europe?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think it is a great irony of the post cold war period that there is less diversity and debate about a range of issues including foreign policy issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In short, no complaint about this, of course, but in short, you are fundamentally a fairly right-wing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't think this is going to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I explain why because I've just come to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your book, as long ago as what, 1994, had a particular acknowledgment to Maja Freundlich, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she was in the HDZ as its vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Was she then its vice-president?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If not then, she has been.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As far as I know, she has only recently become active in the politics of the HDZ within fact literally the last few weeks or two or three months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she is again perhaps on an extreme wing; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think you can have a minority position without, perhaps, being extreme. Extreme implies that you are anti-democratic or something rather than simply one disagrees with, perhaps, the majority position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you, in fact, since the beginning of your work on Yugoslavia had rather close connections with the HDZ, because you actually share some of their political ideology?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have no connections formally speaking with any political party. I've talked with a variety of people from all political parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because I want to you look, please, at one part of your report towards the end where you express, it may be, views that are critical of England or English people. If you go right to the end of your report, 31, I think, will start us off.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we've already dealt with the report so we can probably go to page 32. Incidentally, just before we go to part or finally from the report as at issue, would you accept that at important meetings wherever possible, the British army used where possible its own interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It had, I believe, two native speakers of Serbo-Croat, a certain Islamic who has written his memoirs, as you probably know, or the Court will be aware, Milos Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you accept that one of the most loyal interpreters who was tragically shot was not a Muslim at all, and he was one of the senior interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think I've said that all --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 32, you start dealing with Ahmici. Now, from what you've told us already, there is nothing you can tell us about the events at Ahmici yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Precisely what my report is about is how this was -- this terrible event was presented in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have no, and you don't wish to offer us any personal view on what may have happened there?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think the Court has got vast amounts of evidence from people who are infinitely better qualified than I am to say what happened to cause the horrible amount of murders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the middle of the page, there's this paragraph: "In the days running up to the discovery and the publicity circus surrounding the Ahmici massacre, the Serb offensive around Srebrenica had put reluctant western governments, especially the British one, under pressure to use military force to prevent Serb gains. It was certainly convenient that more than one village should appear on stage to muddy the Bosnian waters." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It means what it says. The British government and other governments who had contributed forces to UNPROFOR, whereas the ministers and so on had publicly stated they did not wish to be drawn into a conflict, no doubt for the reason they did not wish for there to be lightly armed British and other soldiers to be subject to the risks of conflict. At the same time, as I quote further on in the text, because of the Bosnian Serb offensive at Srebrenica, there was a very considerable clamour in the British parliament and in other places, in other governments, and also in the British press. It clearly was not to the advantage of the Bosnian Serbs to face an intervention by NATO forces which might -- those forces on the ground might be lightly armed and ill-equipped, but others might be drawn in who were much heavily armed and better equipped. I simply mean that this horrible massacre was something that caused, despite, no doubt, their dislike or horror at the actual events, certain relief that that public pressure would be relieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We must look at what follows. The rest of page 32, page 33, and over to 34, sets out all about the revelations. You may not have got it accurate, but it sets out what you know about the revelations of Ahmici and when it came to be broadcast and publicised. You're suggesting there a delay in publication. What is true as opposed to the unstated nature of your allegation, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] -- that there was a delay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But what's --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Well, that, for instance, the press were then taken to the site and that the reading of the consequences of this massacre from the point of view of the global conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that involving the Bosnian Serbs, was now converted because this became the main issue in the media; and other issues, particularly the Bosnian Serb offensive around Srebrenica was pushed onto the back burner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I dare say. But what I want to know is: What are you seeking to say about any underlying pulling of strings, if this is your case, that led to a delay in reporting?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I think -- the point was that although the event had taken place, as far as I can tell, several days before the media had access to the site with, presumably, their various satellite dishes and other things to directly report it, that the British government, as I say, in a sense, because it confirmed their argument -- they have, of course, had this argument, you know. It was to some extent a confirmation of their argument that one could not regard a particular party to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina as being overwhelmingly responsible and therefore perhaps a suitable subject for international intervention against it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that would not favour delay in -- sorry. I'll just wait. But that's not going to favour delay in reporting. And because I don't want to take too long over this, will you please go on page 34 to the first fresh paragraph, which begins: "Even Lord Owen ..." And the last four lines of that paragraph says as follows: "The coincidence of the discovery of the Ahmici massacre, with the crescendo of international concern about the fate of Srebrenica and the dilemma posed especially to the British government as the major force provider for UNPROFOR, along with France, was painfully obvious at the time." Well, now, I want to know, please, first of all, obvious to whom? Second, you've spent whatever it is, a couple of pages, and more, setting out simply a history of observations and then saying that the discovery is painfully obvious and is a coincidence. What are you really saying here? Anything?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that in April of 1993 the governments who provided the forces to UNPROFOR felt themselves under a great deal of pressure to intervene militarily, which they did not wish to do. Until the outbreak of conflict between the Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, and until particularly this crime in Ahmici, the argument which had been repeatedly put forward by government spokesmen in Britain, ministers and others, that all sides in the Balkans were much of a muchness and equally responsible, was increasingly fraying precisely because there had not been an atrocity of the sort that occurred. Now, you might say to me, therefore, I am proven wrong to say that the Serbs are primarily responsible. What I'm saying is that this tragic and horrible event was certainly used and presented in the media as an explanation as to why those people who felt that intervention to stop the conflict were wrong. I quote, I think, Sir Malcolm Refkin making the point that those who said, "Raise the arms embargo to assist the Muslims" would now find themselves providing weapons to people fighting as if via a secondary civil war. And with regard to the delay, I imagine that that revolved around technical issues, but you could say that it was obviously an important point, and certainly the event was horrible, that the British armed forces facilitated the exposure of this event, this evidence, televisual evidence, in the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be, would you accept this, that but for people like Martin Bell and Bob Stewart, the Croats would never have divulged what happened in Ahmici at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's a matter of comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go please, then, to the last paragraph on page 34 and help us with that. I'm going to come back to what you said above about coincidence. "Any understanding of the tragic events of mid-April cannot take at face value the assertions of any of the participants. All of them," and you then say this, "including quite clearly the British military participants in UNPROFOR, had, and may well still have, political agendas of their own. Bias there was, certainly enough, on all sides. To privilege the testimony of any one set of participants as ex officio reliable and to fly in the face of the evidence." Well, please, what are you suggesting there? And in particular, what, if anything, are you suggesting about either the reliability of British UNPROFOR witnesses or the British who reported Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As I explained earlier, I think there are -- bias is not necessarily a conscious form of dishonesty, that is the first point. Secondly, as I've just explained, it was the official line, not only of the British government but, by extension, expected of British military participants that they should not say or do anything that obviously went against British policy. In a free society it's perfectly reasonable for me, for citizens to criticise a policy. Obviously, military personnel are put in a difficult position if they do not necessarily agree with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You no more have a shred of evidence to suggest bias by military observers than you have a shred of evidence to suggest, in some way, distortion by interpreters, do you? You don't have a shred of evidence of either?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I think I've said earlier that I -- there is evidence, for instance, in Colonel Stewart's book, his understanding of the background of the conflict as opposed to his description of events. I think the result is simplistic and in that sense biased, but I'm not impugning His Honour. It seems to me it is possible to be patriotic and not necessarily agree with the government policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to press you once more because of what you've said in your report.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have a shred of evidence to suggest bias by the observers in what they reported any more than you have a shred of evidence to suggest the effect or affect by the interpreters, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There is the implication that in certain of his statements to the press after the event, Colonel Stewart says that he's not sure who's done it, then he becomes sure. But since, I'm glad to say, none of these participants are -- have been accused of anything, then my opinion about their -- how they form their opinions may be less than relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, before I turn to the next topic, is this the high point of your case, because an officer who was contemporaneously investigating events may have changed from uncertainty to certainty as his investigation unfolded? That's the high point of your case, is it, on bias?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There is a great deal of evidence of, as I said, about how the forces went to Bosnia-Herzegovina were briefed, what sort of information they would be given, including by a subsequent member of the government in Pale. That created an atmosphere of bias. There was then the problem that it was quite clear that the British government did not wish to see any kind of active military intervention and was very critical of anybody who proposed this. In a small army like the British army, it would be evident to anybody what the political masters, who were, of course, the elected government, wished and did not wish to be promoted as a policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to deal with that any further, thank you. What was the HZ HB, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The -- the -- of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm struggling to find the correct word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've got something to read so let me catch up. Take your time. Sorry. You write about the HZ HB so I wonder if you could tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Sorry, I have suffered a mental blank. Would you draw my attention to the page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh yes, of course. You can see it on page 28.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I was talking about the Croatian Community as I think it's generally translated. These were these institutions that were created at the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just let's see what they were, first, and when they were created. Now, you didn't know, when I initially asked you. You couldn't remember. Can we look at page 20, as well keeping our fingers in page 28.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You set out at the foot of page 20 an extended quotation from the passage from Dr. --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Malcolm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's actually an account of somebody else but it sets out what Dr. Malcolm -- and it then says at the foot of that page, "The Croat counterpart, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was not proclaimed until July 1992 after three months of Serbian military offensive in Bosnia." Malcolm continues, "The Croats of Herzegovina have some reason to be more hard-lined." And you then say in your next paragraph, "Furthermore, even Dr. Malcolm, whom I regard as the best-informed and most eloquent of the proponents of Bosnian statehood admits that after they had been joined," and so on. So that's something that was created in July 1992 and on page 28, you're referring to HZ Herceg-Bosna created on the 18th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand it, there were these preliminary Croatian communities in 1991, but that the, if you like, subpolitical entity that linked the Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is conventionally referred to as Herceg-Bosna which would include the area of discussion that then formed later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So what was the purpose and the function of this earlier body that you describe as a subpolitical entity, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As I understand it, the event -- in these events in November 1991, when the Serbian forces were still besieging Vukovar and so on, as a preparation for a potential conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whose future status was not resolved and Croatian groups organise themselves at a political and at a preparatory, military level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you any knowledge of, and have you taken account of meetings in June of 1991 which preceded the creation of these subpolitical entities, what it is, the 16th and 20th of June? Do you know anything about those meetings at all?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No, but from the dates you give, they follow the Serb union of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if these were meetings in Zagreb where different factions of the local HDZ, the Bosnian HDZ were being sounded out by Tudjman, they might be very important, mightn't they? You know nothing about them at all.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have seen no documentation on them, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this subpolitical entity, if it was an HDZ entity should, of course, have been presided over, for example, Kljuic, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It might have been. I don't know necessarily if it should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can't help the Chamber at all with how it might have come about that Kljuic was kept unaware of the creation of this event?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I do not know if he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can we look, please, very briefly, I'm sorry that it's been taken away, but Exhibit 2717 which is a document we know you've reviewed in full. And we can just literally put page 13 on the ELMO, although -- no, perhaps better look at the page 12 for its context. Mr. Almond, this is the same meeting with Tudjman and Kljuic and all sorts of others, and what happens is as you can see on page 12, that Kostroman took the minutes of -- let me make sure I've got this right myself -- took the minutes and went through them. And then over the page at page 13, this is the minutes of an earlier meeting of something called Herceg-Bosna, and here there are two passages that may be interesting. "Item 2, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna has once again confirmed the will of the entire Croatian people of Herceg-Bosna expressed on 18 November 1991 in Grude, taking the historic decision to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which serves as a legal basis for the entry of these territories into the Republic of Croatia." Now, what on earth do you make of that, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: That these decision in November of 1991 were based upon the situation that then existed, that is to say, of a conflict between the Serbs and the Croats, large parts of Croatia being occupied, and the lack of clarity about the future status of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that for many Croats, particularly those who were no doubt supporters of the HDZ, that in the event of the breakup of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there should be an unification and that seemed to be happening. What is striking is that it doesn't happen afterwards. There isn't, in fact, an annexation or integration, whatever the aspiration is to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well let's just, before we part from this, remind you through the Chamber, Karadjordjevo, two meetings with Tudjman and the factions of the HDZ of which you are unaware, and then this meeting shortly after the creation of this subpolitical group where the subpolitical group speaks in terms of serving as a basis for entry into the territories of the Republic of Croatia. Would you look at item three as well? "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna recognises the full legitimacy of Dr. Franjo Tudjman ..." cut a few words, "... to promote the interests of the Croatian community both among international factors and during interparty and interrepublic agreements on the establishment of the final borders of the Republic of Croatia." You don't, by any chance, think that this reflects an understanding by parties on all sides that partition or annexation, were it to have happened, could be entrusted to Dr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: The representation of their interests, because as you slightly omitted, he's a leader of the political party, Dr. Tudjman as with Milosevic, as head of state of one country, was, of course, repeatedly invited to negotiations and ultimately acted as the representative at Dayton so that in the -- in this particular context, this anticipates a role that was later to become explicit in relation to the International Community, and it refers to interparty and interrepublic agreements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so I understand it, you not having looked at this in detail before, but your, as it were, off-the-cuff explanation is that we should not now interpret this because Dr. Tudjman is head of the party not because he's head of state; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: He's head of Croatia but, of course, there was a political party as was the case with several other instances which cut across boundaries. The HDZ was not unique in this factor and I think the construction that you are putting on it or the prosecution is putting a construction that this necessarily implies a partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the will of its inhabitants as opposed to an argument that if Bosnia-Herzegovina is not going to survive, primarily as a result of the Serb actions, was it not normal and reasonable that Croatians, particularly those who belong to the same political party, looked to Tudjman as their leader and respective? And as I say, in a variety of international mediation efforts and at Dayton, Tudjman was treated in that way as Milosevic was treated as the representative of Serbs; not always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have no further explanation to give as between what was created in November 1991 and what was created in July 1992. You have no further knowledge beyond what you've already given us?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Nothing that would further my argument -- alter my argument.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so on the same page, you will have noticed -- just draw it to your attention and the Judges through you, "Item 4, President Boban and vice-presidents Rajic and Kordic and secretary Kostroman authorised to represent, with full legitimacy, a Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at the meeting in Zagreb on the 27th of December." What do you say to all that? Does that help you with understanding what you're dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: They are authorised by that meeting to be -- sorry, that they are authorised to be the representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zagreb. Very well, I'm going to move on because I want to know the answer to the next question. Now, you said this morning in answer to a question by His Honour, Judge Robinson, I think, that the fighting was produced by contingent events after the war broke out. When did the war break out on your analysis?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: War between the Bosnian Serbs and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I think --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Do you mean the war between --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the fighting between the Croats and the Muslims. I may be wrong. I've tried to --

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: My point was that the -- in the lead up and the intensification of bad relations from the winter of 1992 to the events which are the subject of this trial primary, the growing pressure of refugees and also Bosnian army units to have been displaced produced these tensions which then led to conflicts including -- where the context of the particular events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the contingent events, are they, refugees, matters of that sort and displaced army units?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Competition for space, for lodging, for food, for supply lines. The fears of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: None of this excludes the necessity for there being a mind behind a controlling mind or minds behind the military actions that took place, does it?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There were minds behind the military actions on both sides. It's clear why they took the decisions they did. I, myself, find it difficult to take the view of -- that this conflict was carefully planned over -- by this time, approximately two years, because of the surrounding events, and the surrounding geopolitical strategic position of the Croats and also of the Bosnian Muslims. It is really to the advantage of neither to have this conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it may have turned out, but your -- you've got to go back in time. You can't help us, one way or another, with whether it was planned, how long it was planned, by whom it was planned, by whom it was executed, can you, on either side?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There are better witnesses, including the active participants than me, quite obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But more than that, just to finish with this point, as someone whose expertise, as you have told us, is only concerned with the external assessment by Europeans and others of events, of course, you can't help us with what actually happened inside, can you?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: My primary focus was on the external events and the intervention of the International Community, but of course one would have to try as best one could to follow the events and they were extremely confusing and I think remain still unclarified. That is the point, surely, of this trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't suggest that you have any expertise, just to be quite sure, you don't suggest you have any expertise to unravel that list of things I suggested to you, whether it was planned, when, by whom, and who executed it. You don't have any expertise in that area at all, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I have nothing to offer, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please -- if you've still got that document if the usher would be good enough, turn it to page 10. On page 10, I'm sorry. Your Honour, would you give me one moment? My mistake. Will you just give me one moment, please. Can we go to page 60 of this report. I'm sorry if I was in error.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: May I keep page 10?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the Chamber is becoming concerned at the length of the cross-examination. We believe you have gone on sufficiently long and you should bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was bringing it to a close in any event. This is either my last or penultimate topic?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: May I just draw the attention of The Bench to the paragraph -- the second paragraph of Mate Boban's intervention which I think supports the tenure of my interpretation, but I don't want to drag out the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Since you've made the point, let's see where it is.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: He says, half way through that paragraph, as reported, "Should Bosnia-Herzegovina remain an independent state without any ties with the former disintegrating or future -- or should Bosnia itself disintegrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Hold on. Can we go up on the ELMO. There we are. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: "The area where about 650.000 Croats live would implement internationally recognised democratic methods proclaiming this to be independent Croatian territory."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next sentence as well, or next phrase.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: "Which will exceed the state of Croatia but only at such time as the Croatian leadership, in whom our people until now have placed their complete trust should decide the moment and the time had come." But in this presumably private meeting, there is a reference to democratic methods and disintegration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now go to page 60. Here we have President Tudjman addressing Kljuic, and I'm going to go straight to the first -- the next complete, very short paragraph. He says this: "Therefore, we finally wanted, and it was no accident, that in the preamble to the Croatian constitution we also mention the banovina of Croatia." And if, with that passage in mind, you'd turn to page 10 of your report. In the middle of the page you set this out: "The August '39 agreement between the leading Croat politician Madzek [phoen] and the Serbian prime minister, which effectively conceded a large part of Bosnia to a new Croatian unit within a reformed Yugoslavia has a special significance because the boundaries delineated then played such a role in the thinking behind the Vance-Owen Plan and debates about it in the spring of 1993." The banovina was critically important as Lord Owen said, and it's quoted in Dr. Donia's report, had crucial significance so far as Tudjman was concerned and other Croats, because that's what they were aiming for. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier in my oral evidence, I believe that a large number of Croats regarded that settlement, which was a constitutional deal, not the product of force, as being, from the point of view of their nation, an ideal solution. I don't think that to say that Tudjman or other Croats necessarily wished to revert to that model implies the conspiracy, the collusion, the persistent, as it were, cooperation with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have, since this morning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I do have since this morning a draft translation of the Kiseljak documents to which I referred and of course which have only come into our possession recently. I'm pretty well neutral as to whether I put them to this witness, although I've asked him about them, or whether I put them to another witness or introduce them in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the matter has been taken far enough for today. You can deal with it at a future date. Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Browning:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
