utterances.text: Mr. Almond, let me first of all start where the Prosecution left off, with Prosecution Exhibit 2717A, which you should have in front of you. Let's put this in its appropriate historical context. That document is dated December 27th, or refers to a meeting of December 27th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the referendum for independence in Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been February 29th and March 1, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It took place later, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this document, this meeting, was roughly three months before the fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been determined?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. And the pace of events, of course, meant that those periods seemed no doubt like a lifetime to many people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of this meeting, what would happen with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina was very much up in the air, both within the country as well as in the eyes of the International Community?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. The United States, for instance, had not followed the majority of European Community states in recognising either Slovenia or Croatia at this stage, and therefore the acceptance of Bosnia-Herzegovina into the International Community as a normally recognised sovereign state was, I believe, far from clear-cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the referendum of March 1, 1992, was there any indication that President Tudjman and President Milosevic ever met to discuss a possible partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: I don't know of any meeting to discuss that. Of course, they met frequently, relatively frequently, under the auspices of various international mediation efforts. They may also have spoken on the telephone, as did other leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was certainly no indication of a discussion concerning partition after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No. And as I emphasise in my report, the criticism of Tudjman made at home was that he was failing to resist or to reverse the occupation of Croatian territory, let alone the Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the referendum of February 29th and March 1, 1992, was it certain that Bosnia-Herzegovina would opt for independence?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It was not certain, no, and nor necessarily was it welcome to the International Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen any indication that President Tudjman at any point ever advocated the use of force to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No. The evidence of actions is that eventually he used force to prevent the overrunning of the Bosnian Muslim side and also Bosnian Croats in the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was put to you that Karadjordjevo involved discussions about what would happen to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time of Karadjordjevo, of the meeting in Karadjordjevo, was Bosnia-Herzegovina a state, as put to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It was a constituent republic of the Yugoslav Socialist Federal Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of whether it would become an independent state, that was very much an open question at the time of Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It was an open question, and also both European Community political leaders and the United States vigorously discouraged the independence of any of these republics, or the seeking of independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Karadjordjevo, shortly after Karadjordjevo, in August of 1991, there was a full-scale attack by Serbia upon the Republic of Croatia, was there not?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Starting even before then, yes, in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does that -- what should one take from that with respect to whether there was an agreement that had been reached at Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It would be a most peculiar deal whereby Croatia did not gain any territory in Bosnia but lost about 30 per cent of its own territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been shown a map from a banquet at the meeting between Paddy Ashdown and President Tudjman. Did that -- were the words of President Tudjman, his description that this is what Bosnia-Herzegovina might look like in ten years, was that what was reported or made available in the press?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: President Tudjman, to the best of my knowledge, his comments, to the best of my knowledge, whatever they may have been, have only been reported indirectly through the recollection of Paddy Ashdown. The map itself is interesting, because of course the writing on it is obviously, however accurate, subsequent. But if you look at the map itself, it, for instance, leaves no space for the Krajina Serb military forces, and I think therefore my suggestion that President Tudjman presumably, as commander-in-chief of the Croatian army at that time, was anticipating what we know was to happen within a few weeks -- within a few days, I should say, in Slovenia, western Slovenia, and then in the Krajina, a military operation against the Serbs, which culminated in the assistance to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Bosnian Serbs in August and afterwards of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Croatia was the first country to recognise the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that step of recognising the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there any effort made by Croatia in any way to annex a portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: There was no annexation of territory, even when the powerless military position of the Bosnian government forces would have made it very easy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to wrap up very quickly, but I do want to ask you about another Prosecution Exhibit that you were shown, Z92.1, which was -- and I think it's referred to as an alleged agreement of May 7th, 1992. Shortly after that meeting, did Serbs attack Bosnian Croats in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: Yes. I think this agreement was like, sadly, even those agreements mediated by the International Community, a dead letter, and indeed that's why I could not imagine that there was any cooperation very frequently. Not least, the Bosnian Serbs agreed to agree to make -- score points in the media, score points with public opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you refer to it as an agreement, but do you have any reason to believe it's anything more than an alleged agreement?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: It's certainly not an agreement that had any effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were subjected to an extensive amount of questions during cross-examination and shown several pieces of paper, but have any of your opinions changed as a result of any of the material that you were shown here in Court today?

utterances.speaker: MARK ALMOND
utterances.text: No. I still -- the evidence seems to me to reinforce the point that in this tragic situation, as Yugoslavia broke up and the Serb government and forces pursued their own goals by military force, that various options were open to discussion, but nothing that I would regard as criminal or conspiratorial was ever implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Almond. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Almond, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Dr. Stjepan Mestrovic is available. He's an expert witness addressing the sociological opinions produced by the Prosecution. And with the Court's permission, as I've stated, Mr. Browning will lead his evidence too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll sit till 4.15 and see if we can finish his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour -- oh, he's coming in. I was just going to raise a couple of timetable matters. I can do them at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, can you speak into the microphone more? I have trouble hearing you, but I understand that others are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do my best to speak up, and I'll do my best to pause as well. I've been sufficiently warned by co-counsel. Examined by Mr. Browning:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mestrovic, could I have you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Gabriel Mestrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't want to dwell on your experience and background, but there are a few points that I would like to highlight briefly. You have three degrees from Harvard University?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and one of them is a master's in theological studies which dealt with the world's religions and their import and their meaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also have a Ph.D. from Syracuse?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: In sociology, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are a series editor on eastern Europe?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a series on eastern Europe at Texas A & M University Press. At the time we established it in 1992, it was one of only a handful of such series. The other major one was Duke University Press and we published over 15 treatises on communist and post-communist developments in eastern Europe ranging from Poland, Hungary, the Ukraine, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're a full-write scholar?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of the first full-write scholars in newly established Croatia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many books have you published?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: A total of 14 books that I published or edited, and of these I believe about four or five have to do in some way with the Balkans or this current war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also published a number of prestigious journals?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a flavour for those publications?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: In "The Chronicle of Higher Education," I talked about why eastern Europe's upheavals caught people off guard when communism began to collapse. In "The International Journal of Law and Psychiatry," I discussed issues of the dangerousness standard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Browning, I think you have to change the place of your microphone, because if you manage to -- no. Like Mr. Nice, you know. It has to be just in front of you, otherwise you cannot -- otherwise we don't hear you very well. That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mestrovic, you have appeared on CNN as well as national public radio. I'd like for you to describe those appearances, but first of all could you explain what national public radio is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: It is a prestigious non-profit national radio network in the United States, something in the order of the prestige of the BBC, and I've discussed on it my books, ranging from "Habits of the Balkan Heart" to -- there was one appearance about the significance of the death of Milovan Djilas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you currently live in the United States?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With citizenship in the United States?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a United States citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you move from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: In 1963, when I was 8 years old, I moved to the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report that you have prepared and filed in this matter, is that report a full and accurate summary of your opinions and conclusions in this matter?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you actually prepared that report yourself, did you not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber the concept of ethnic distance as a sociological term?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: It is a concept that was invented in the 1920s at the University of Chicago Department of Sociology and it has been used in research all over the world since then. And basically it measures the degree to which ordinary people feel close or distant to people of other ethnic groups and is measured by questions asked them: Well, would you want the person of a different ethnic group as your neighbour or as a friend or someone to marry, and other questions of that sort. So it's a very good indicator of tolerance or intolerance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain specifically how that is measured? I take it it's some sort of survey that is conducted to measure ethnic distance.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a quantitative scale and it is administered and carefully designed random samples so that social scientists are able to make valid and accurate generalisations from it, and it is used in conjunction with other variables in quantitative analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain how ethnic distance changed in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain it in terms of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but certainly Croatia. There was research conducted using the ethnic distance scale in Croatia in 1984, and then repeated throughout Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1989. So a point of comparison is only for Croatia in terms of the two time periods, 1984 and 1989. What that aspect of the research shows, and it's been published by various collaborators who were in this consortium, and they include Dusko Sekulic, Mladen Lazic, and Vjeran Katunaric, among others, but what it shows is that ethnic distance did rise in Croatia between those two time points, 1984 and 1989, and the significance of that, I think, is that it arose prior to the rise of Franjo Tudjman to power, political power, and it arose during the communist era.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that empirical data something that you would expect a sociologist to look to and to turn to and to rely upon in evaluating the conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I think first of all it speaks directly to the issues that are before this Tribunal. Second, the research that has been published by Dusko Sekulic was published in the three most prestigious journals in the United States in sociology -- namely, the American Journal of Sociology in 1994, the American Sociological Review in 1994, and Social Forces in 1999 -- which the fact that these are highly prestigious journals, the fact they went through a peer review process, the fact that we can be certain that they would not have been published unless they had gone through rigorous examinations, does lend a great amount of validity to their findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does this empirical data show you, as a sociologist, about the rise of nationalism in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, contrary to the assertions made by Dr. Allcock in his expert report, who claimed that there was a process which he calls ethnogenesis, by which he means that Franjo Tudjman somehow single-handedly engineered or produced ethnic tension in Croatia, what the data suggests is that prior to Franjo Tudjman even being on the scene, the sense of ethnic distance arose of its own accord, from the bottom up, and whatever factors led to it certainly they were not and cannot be attributed to Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to agreeing to serve as an expert witness in this case, had you had any knowledge or interaction with Dr. Allcock?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: No, I had not heard of him before this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Trial Chamber the differences between the conclusions that you reached and those of Dr. Allcock?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Allcock does not cite the studies that I've cited, which are empirical. He does not cite very many studies at all. So his report really contains many assertions that are unsubstantiated. So the major difference between us is that he asserts but does not substantiate the claim that Franjo Tudjman engaged in what he calls ethnogenesis, whereas I seek to suggest, using empirical data, that whatever may have occurred in the former Yugoslavia, it had to do with social structures and social forces that came from the bottom up and were independent of Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the witness. He said "from the bottom up." What does he mean by saying social forces which came from the bottom up? Historically speaking, could you tell us what does he take as his point of departure? When is it that this ethnic opposition began to emerge? Could he give us any dates? Because there must be a certain historical period to which one could -- with which one could associate this ethnic opposition that you believe to be independent from Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there will be several dimensions to these social structures. One is a history in which the various ethnic communities lived together physically, socially in worlds apart, segregated in the worlds unto themselves. There was a certain amount of tolerance but there was not understanding, there was not compassion. So one structural factor is a state in which you have ethnic groups living side by side but not interpenetrating each other. Another structural factor would be, and this is brought out correctly by Dr. Allcock in some of his other writings, namely that the communist regime simultaneously promoted ethnic divisions at the same time that it tried to obliterate them. So in the name of brotherhood and unity, one was supposed to think of oneself as a Yugoslav and not as a Croat or Serb or Bosnian Muslim. At the same time they allowed, condoned, and even promoted such ethnic divisions. So these ethnic divisions were present in the consciousness of the people. And third, what I mean by "bottom up", is that in every day interaction, despite the repression of the Tito regime, people noticed, as this research showed, people noticed that in Croatia, for example, the Serbs were getting the most prestigious and largest apartments. They noticed that the Serbs in Croatia were being promoted in the rank of general, and in the JNA, and Croats tended not to be. People noticed that the size of apartments, jobs, other factors among themselves; talking, gossiping, this was occurring. So despite the official party line of brotherhood and unity, there were perceptions, and I think this research shows that when you asked ordinary people what they thought and what they felt, these perceptions came through regardless of the official propaganda line from the capital of Yugoslavia. So I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not quite. That question was not whether there was social, and I think the difference is we know that they did, but whether new nationalism which emerged with the end of the cold war and this new nationalism and nationalism, the nationalism Croat or rather the renaissance of this nationalism, did it rely on this ethnic differentiation and then imposed itself and tried to impose a new state. Because this is the thesis which was profounded here, that it was -- this nationalism was the factor which reactivated because it was reactivated because it was dormant and, in a way, incited or promoted in other ways in order to then be used politically and to be imposed politically in a different state structure. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the data shows and not just in the former Yugoslavia, but in general, that nationalism wrecked or helped to tear down communism. Communism did not fall apart from its own accord. The nationalism arose partly sociologically speaking because the nations that had communism did not have a tradition such as we have in the west of the reformation of the Bill of Rights, of other traditions that promote human rights and individual rights. They were much more traditional societies that, for the most part, did not undergo these developments. Therefore, structurally speaking, as people began to notice inconsistencies, hypocrisies and exploitation in communism, the only fall back position that they had, given that they did not have these western traditions, was nationalism. Furthermore, at the same time that this was occurring, the west was undergoing a sort of chaotic state of its own. It was caught off guard by the developments. The west wanted to preserve, in 1991, the integrity of the Soviet Union out of its own fears of nuclear weapons and so forth, and the west did not know what to offer these new emerging republics. So a vacuum was created in which formerly communist nations were looking to the west that was not prepared to give them guidance and nationalism was, so to speak, the logical alternative. But my point is that this nationalism arose from a bottom up as a way to fill this vacuum precisely because there was no top down or centre guidance not only within these nations but also in the west which was reacting in a very confused timid manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could one then say, sir, that you associate yourself with a doctrine or a sociological school of thought which is called structuralism; do you associate with it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have used it. In that sense, I belong to it. I certainly have used other sociological theories as well but it's fair to characterise me as a structuralist, functionalist, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this doctrine, does it attach less importance to the individual's will and leaders and much more to the social structure; is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. In fact, this theory tends to say that so-called leaders are produced by the group on the spur of the moment as opposed to a doctrine that says that the leader is the one that is producing changes in the social group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mestrovic, is it, if I could ask you to turn to the conclusions of Dr. Donia, and if you could summarise the opinions and conclusions that you reach that differ from those of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Donia's central assertion seems to be that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a peaceful and multi-ethnic nation for centuries, many centuries, and again, prior to the rise of Franjo Tudjman. Moreover, he asserts that there was no violence that could be attributed to ethnic differences in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what I point out in my report goes contrary to Dr. Donia, is that even in his writings, which are not used in his report, he does cite ethnic violence in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Moreover, other historians and experts on this region point to a history replete with insurrections and with ethnic conflict. So contrary to Dr. Donia's assertions, I would claim that the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina is one of recurrent ethnic tensions and wars and insurrections, and in this way I differ very sharply with his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Donia is a historian and you are a sociologist. Why is it that you address the opinions and conclusions of a historian?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in his -- I believe it's page four of his book with Dr. Fine, he says that he's not doing conventional history in the sense of offering a chronology or analysing events; that he's making generalisations, generalisations that are not characteristic of historians. So in that sense, he is entering the domain or the purview of sociologists, and I take him up to the extent that he enters the sociological domain. For example, I note in my report that in his report he condenses a lot of history, contemporary history, in 1991, 1992, in just a few pages, when the chronology as I use in the Carnegie Commission and draws out some of those events, things that happened, that really would have been more appropriate for a historian. So to answer your question, it is because I think he deviates from conventional history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Forgive me for oversimplifying, but I believe your report also addresses the way the world is viewed or the events are viewed by the culture in the United States and western Europe versus the way the world is viewed within the Balkans. Could you elaborate upon that concept, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sociologists are very sensitive to perceptions and particularly how western perceptions sometimes impinge upon or obscure how non-western cultures see themselves or see the world. And one of the things that I would note as a sociologist is that in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief, as well as in the expert testimonies of Dr. Allcock and Dr. Donia, there is a constant reliance upon the theme of planning, coordination, being systematic, and things of that sort that really bespeak a certain rational mindset that is taken for granted in the west but that is less likely or is more problematic in non-western cultures. So I accentuate a source of cultural bias in approaching this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mestrovic, if I could ask you to very briefly summarise the conclusions that you've come to based upon sociological principles and the empirical data that you've relied upon as set out in your report.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I rely upon empirical research conducted by Dusko Sekulic, Mladen Lazic, Vjeran Katunaric, and others from this consortium to which I referred to earlier, which suggests that ethnic distance rose in Croatia between 1984 and 1989 from the bottom up, if you will, certainly prior to the rise of Franjo Tudjman. I cite sources that are not cited by Dr. Donia, including some of his own writings, which suggest there was plenty of ethnic conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I bring up research again by Sekulic which suggests that intolerance and violence are not necessarily related, that the most intolerant republics in the former Yugoslavia were Kosovo and Slovenia, which escaped, at that time, anyway, most of the violence, but the most tolerant republic was Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was plunged into the most brutal violence. So that one has to carefully examine the situation concepts, which seem to be taken for granted and not substantiated by the expert witnesses for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BROWNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Mestrovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer to start tomorrow, but I'm entirely in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can make a start to save some time tomorrow, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether there are any witnesses tomorrow, but in any event. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mestrovic, what is the significance for the findings of a court looking at the actions of individuals in 1993 of the findings that you say you made?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: The significance is that your expert witnesses have not proved that these individuals could have engineered the so-called ethnogenesis which is attributed to them in the light of generally accepted sociological principles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what people prove is ultimately a matter for the Judges. Are you saying that by reason of these cultural differences and by reason of the bottom-up potential for nationalism and so on to arise, these individuals aren't capable of planning, aren't capable of organising? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, explain then how, to recast your answer, these sociological or cultural differences are likely to impede the process and proof of planning, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm responding to the arguments made by your expert witnesses, and I'm saying that the way they set forth the argument that Franjo Tudjman could have engineered this ethnogenesis is not substantiated by research that shows that the ethnic distance had arose prior to his being on the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll explore tomorrow, in more detail, what the particular propositions that we are advancing or that the witnesses are advancing are. I come back to the first question. What you offer in your report doesn't, in any sense, render it impossible for people to have planned the things as part of the Prosecution's case said were planned?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Impossible, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that by reason of cultural differences, in some way it's less likely for people like Tudjman to plan something because he's culturally incapable of doing it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Not quite in that way, because you're talking about him as an individual. What I am saying is that the culture in the entire former Yugoslavia would make the level of systemisation, coordination, planning, and so forth which you an attribute to any of the actors more problematic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, I think I'd like some more help on that, because it's all my ignorance of your particular area, but there's a difficulty -- you're really asserting that as one crosses from Austria into the former Yugoslavia, or from one bit of the former Yugoslavia into another, we are passing from a population that can easily plan wars and deceptions and so on into a population that is less able to do that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. What I'm claiming is that there are standard books in sociology, such as Zygmunt Bauman's "Modernity and the Holocaust" which claim, for example, that the German people could and did engage in widespread and systematic genocide because they had already had a cultural proclivity and a structure that was suited towards bureaucracy, efficiency, rationalisation, coordination. And we do know, for example, that the Holocaust continued as a very systematic pace regardless of other events that were occurring around them. And that when one goes further to the east, yes, of course there will be mass killings, there will be planning, there will be actions taken, but they will not be able to take on that same degree of coordination, planning, and efficiency, or it will be more difficult for them to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To take a quite specific point, then, are you saying that for a political leader, it would be more difficult for a political leader, say, to be devious in Bosnia to the extent of doing one thing in public and another thing in private?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: I have to say that sociology has nothing to say on being devious, so I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we've mercifully not had to deal in detail with the organisation of camps and so on in this particular case. This is not a matter in issue. Are you saying that really the camps would be less capable or less liable to be well organised in this territory than they could be well organised as places of punishment or of execution in Germany?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I always want to rely on empirical evidence. The only one book in English is called "The Tenth Circle of Hell," by Hakunovic, in which he experienced at Omarska. And Eli Wiesel, in the preface to this book, says that despite the horrors that occurred in Omarska, Omarska was not Auschwitz. And the descriptions in this book, "The Tenth Circle of Hell," do suggest that the way the brutalities were carried on by the Serbs were not in the same style of efficiency and coordination which you describe. For example, the descriptions by the survivors suggest that the Serbs got drunk at night, they would drink a lot of slivovitz, they would randomly pick certain inmates who they would beat that night. But there was not a rational systematic quota of how many deaths would occur night after night. So all I'm saying is when one goes by the empirical evidence that's out there -- and I submit to you "The Tenth Circle of Hell," it's a very important document for giving us insight into the how the Serbs actually conducted one of these camps -- it does suggest differences, cultural differences, in how murder is carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can all understand how, for example, any culture with alcohol consumption, particularly if it's permitted to operate in this environment, might play havoc on efficiency. But if we omit alcohol and we are dealing with people of intelligence, is there any reason why those people shouldn't be able to plan and organise events much the same way as soldiers or politician in other countries?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, the very fact that such huge amounts of alcohol were encouraged and allowed bespeaks a difference culturally in that intemperance is allowed in these camps among the guards and the inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My mistake. Let's move from the camps, because we've dealt with that, and come back to the circumstances of the individual politician and the individual military leader. If there's no evidence that one or other of those is subject to alcohol excess, is there any cultural reason why either one of such hypothetical figures is going to be less capable of organising, planning, executing plans than people in Britain or America?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the individual leader will not be biologically nor innately different from any other leader in the world. What will be different are the cultural and structural resources available to that leader. That is what a sociologist will immediately point out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that, I think, there's a suggestion from somewhere on the Prosecution side -- it may be from me, I don't know, one of our witnesses, or from Mr. Allcock. You say that we are suggesting that ethnic tension was deliberately engineered by the late President Tudjman. Where do you find that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: It is in the section in which Dr. Allcock introduces the concept of ethnogenesis and then later on links it to the actions in his report of Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got his report with you so that we can see that? Have you got his report there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May he have a copy, if you've got one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, all we have is a marked-up version, but we're more than happy to show it to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd just take me to the passage so that I can see it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, on page 2, top paragraph: "Ethnic cleansing is not a spontaneous manifestation of the grass roots traditions of ethnic communities as much as an instrument of policy. In the present, as in the past, inter-ethnic hostility and ethnic cleansing have been top-down manipulative features of the policies of political leaders in relation to the building of states rather than bottom-up expressions of sentiment on the part of peoples of the region." And then towards the bottom of that same page: "President Tudjman is explicitly linked as having appeared to have created structures --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness either slow down or have the document on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: "-- those formerly associated with the former federal President Tito, namely, top down and very controlling." And the rest of the report really follows along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's being dealt with at the top of the page, unless I've misunderstood it myself, which is always possible, is that we're dealing with inter-ethnic hostility and ethnic cleansing, aren't we? Those are actions. Isn't that what we're dealing with?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Well, hostility does not necessarily have to be an action. It can certainly be an attitude.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could be, but in the context of this report.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. And of course, for things like ethnic cleansing, things that people do one to another, you do need someone to make the decision, don't you? You're not suggesting, are you, that there was a spontaneous, bottom-up, self-arising exercise of ethnic cleansing going on in any part of this breakup?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was all, where it happened, led by a political or a military leader, or both?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to other mitigating factors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that if -- I note your disagreement for the time being and I'll deal with it more fully perhaps tomorrow. But if hostility could more easily be understood -- I don't say there's anything wrong with the way it's written -- be more easily understood by inter-ethnic hostilities, in the plural, denoting acts of aggression leading indeed to warfare, and there's nothing in this paragraph of Dr. Allcock's report that says that Tudjman is generating, expressly and exclusively, ethnic tension and unhappiness, is there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESTROVIC
utterances.text: Not in this paragraph, but in my report I certainly find passages, when put together, it's very clear that Dr. Allcock is blaming the top, the top being for him Franjo Tudjman, for ethnogenesis. I think this is a very clear point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to accept that, so we're going to have to disagree on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've got one minute of administration as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Mestrovic, we've got to adjourn now. Could you be back, please, tomorrow at half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I must warn you, as I must warn all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to go now, please, and be back at half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of matters of information, really, and to some degree one request. The information is that in relation to Dr. Pavlovic, you'll remember that he's coming along to deal with certain medical issues, and we were asked last week if we could accommodate him today. I made every effort over the weekend and was able to write to Mr. Sayers saying that I couldn't make it today, but I would be able, I think, with luck, to deal with him tomorrow. In the event -- I certainly am in a position to deal with him tomorrow, but I understand now that he won't be coming in till Wednesday, so that can we deal with him then? But it would be inconvenient for it to be beyond Wednesday, because the efforts that I've made to advance my position are such that Wednesday would be about the latest, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very simply, Mr. President, we were led to believe by the Prosecution that they would not be through with even Dr. -- with even Mr. Almond before tomorrow, so it's true that Dr. Pavlovic we had anticipated bringing on Wednesday morning. He doesn't have a cell phone, but we'll try to get him available, I assume, by tomorrow afternoon, if the Prosecution is through by then, if we can get hold of him, and we'll make every effort to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is he here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think he arrived on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing relates to next Monday, when the audiotape expert for the Defence is to be called. Although I'm not sure about it, I think the Dutch expert will be available to assist on that day. He had two other commitments, one another court hearing which he forecast might very well get cancelled. I haven't yet heard that it has. And second, a travel arrangement to a conference which he was prepared to put off in order to assist this Tribunal. I've informed Mr. Sayers of that, at least I've informed him that he's going to be available, and I had asked Mr. Sayers to consider whether, in the circumstances, the possibility of calling both witnesses next Monday, if the Court case is cancelled and if he is available, is something that they could accommodate. Of course, I understand that they have got other witnesses already scheduled and so on, but if I find out this afternoon that the man is available on Monday, I'd like at least consideration to be given to that, because it would be a tidier and more efficient use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make the inquiries and then consider the timetable for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to that particular issue, Your Honour, I may be mistaken about this, but I thought we had already addressed this, and the resolution was that in view of the 21-day rule and the fact that Mr. Koenig is going to be testifying well within the 21-day rule, that July the 24th was reserved as the day upon which the Rijswijk laboratory witnesses would testify, and we've made our plans accordingly. In fact, I think that was what the Court suggested over a week ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't recollect that at the moment. We can look into it. And in any event, we can consider it later in the week when we know what the position is. Are there any other matters? Half past 9.00 tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
